A word about the test, and about honesty

This book prepares you for the Fullstack .NET Engineer / Angular skill test described in the Woven prep guide used by Andela. That guide lists three timed scenarios:

Scenario Time AI Language
Debugging a problem with limited information 35 min not allowed C#
Check which pages users are authorized to access 40 min not allowed C#
Show a user when their account may be compromised 25 min allowed (cite it) Angular

The guide is explicit that the scenarios are confidential, that using someone else’s solution is unacceptable, and that sharing them is not allowed. This book respects that completely. It does not contain the test’s scenarios, does not guess at them, and contains no “answers”. What it contains is a real application, Sentinel, whose features happen to sit in the same three areas, and a method for each area that you can rehearse until it is a habit. When you sit the test, every line you write will be your own.

Two of the three scenarios forbid AI assistance. That matters for how you use this book: type the code yourself, run the labs without a chatbot, and build the reflexes that the test will measure. The third scenario encourages AI and asks you to cite it; Chapter 26 shows how.

Who this book is for

A developer who can already write C# and has met Angular, and who wants to walk into a timed assessment rehearsed rather than hopeful. If you are newer to programming, Appendices A and B cover the fundamentals the prep guide lists (iteration, classes and objects, arrays, lists and dictionaries, converting between types) in the context of this project.

The application is built the way an enterprise system should be built: Clean Architecture, CQRS, vertical slices and SOLID. You do not need any of that to pass a 40-minute exercise. You do need what it teaches: small functions with clear names, decisions written down, edge cases handled on purpose, and tests that prove it. The architecture is the long version of the same discipline the test rewards in miniature.

How to use this book

Every listing in this book is complete and is the file in the repository, inserted at build time; there are no // ... rest of the class elisions in production code. File paths are given as a header above each listing, relative to the repository root, like this:

src/Sentinel.Domain/Access/PermissionEffect.cs 
namespace Sentinel.Domain.Access;

/// <summary>Whether a user-level override adds a permission or takes it away.</summary>
public enum PermissionEffect
{
    Allow,
    Deny
}

Type the code. Reading code produces the feeling of understanding; typing code produces understanding. If you clone the repository instead, at least pause at the end of each chapter and rebuild from memory the shape of what you just read.

The book has five parts:

  • Part I (Chapters 1–3) reads the test like an engineer, introduces the Sentinel domain, and lays out the architecture.
  • Part II (Chapters 4–13) builds the C# back end. Chapter 7 is the heart of the second scenario; Chapter 8 is the server side of the third.
  • Part III (Chapters 14–20) builds the Angular front end. Chapters 17 and 18 are the heart of the third scenario: passing information between components, and displaying dates.
  • Part IV (Chapters 21–24) is the first scenario: a method for debugging with limited information, two reproducible incidents to practise it on, and how to write up what you found for engineers and for people who are not.
  • Part V (Chapters 25–26) is rehearsal: timed katas and drills, a self-review rubric built from the test’s own evaluation criteria, and a test-day checklist.

If your test is in three days, read Chapters 1, 7, 17, 18, 21, 22 and 26, and do the katas in Chapter 25. If it is in three weeks, read everything, in order.

Getting the code

git clone <your copy of this repository> sentinel
cd sentinel
git branch -a        # main, two lab branches, one drill branch

The README at the root explains how to run everything. Chapter 4 does it step by step.

Part I · Orientation

Chapter 1 · Reading the Skill Test Like an Engineer

Most candidates read a prep guide once, skim the bold text, and open the first scenario. That is like reading the acceptance criteria of a ticket after you have written the code. This chapter reads the guide the way you would read a specification, and turns each sentence into a habit you can practise.

1.1 What the guide actually says

Strip the guide to its load-bearing sentences and you get this:

  1. Three scenarios, each with its own timer, inside a 48-hour window. The timers are short (35, 40 and 25 minutes) and they are per scenario. You can rest between scenarios; you cannot rest inside one.
  2. Research is allowed and should be cited. Looking things up is “not a negative”; using a snippet without a link is.
  3. AI is forbidden in two scenarios and encouraged in one. Breaking the rule disqualifies you.
  4. The environment is Qualified, an online IDE. The guide recommends ten minutes trying it first.
  5. Each scenario lists what reviewers look for. Those lists are the marking scheme. Treat them as such.

The guide also says something about the coding scenario that is easy to skim past: if a more advanced concept is beyond you in the time, “use what you know and leave a comment for the reviewer”. That advice tells you the reviewer is a person reading your code with empathy, not a test runner counting green ticks. A working simple solution with a clear comment beats an ambitious broken one, every time.

1.2 The marking scheme, scenario by scenario

Debugging a problem with limited information (35 minutes, C#, no AI)

You receive a bug report from customer support and “will not have all of the information you need”. Reviewers look at:

Criterion The habit that satisfies it Where this book practises it
How do you gather information about a problem in code? Reproduce first; read the code path end to end; use logs and the debugger before you form opinions Chapter 21, both labs
How do you research issues? Search precisely, read primary documentation, cite every source §21.6, §22.5
How do you document your learning so others can benefit? An investigation log written as you go docs/templates/investigation-log.md
How do you communicate technical concepts to other engineers? A blameless write-up: cause, fix, why it was missed, follow-ups Chapter 24
How do you communicate technical concepts to non-engineers? A reply that answers the reader’s actual worry, first, in their words Chapter 24

Notice that three of the five criteria are about writing. Candidates who find the bug in twenty minutes and spend the last fifteen on a two-line note leave most of the marks on the table. Chapter 21 gives you a timetable for the 35 minutes that protects the writing time.

Check which pages users are authorized to access (40 minutes, C#, no AI)

A coding scenario with provided tests. Reviewers look at:

Criterion The habit
Does your code address the core requirements? Restate the requirements as a checklist in a comment before coding
Did you handle edge cases? List them before coding; decide each one; write a test per decision
Are your variable and function names clear? Name by intent: CanOpen(page), not Check(p)
Is the structure good? Functions right-sized? Anything hard-coded? One public entry point, small private helpers, constants named
Did you add helpful tests beyond the ones provided? Every edge-case decision gets a test
Do you leave helpful comments explaining trade-offs? A short “Decisions” comment at the top of the class

The domain is authorisation: users, pages, and who may open what. Sentinel is built around exactly that problem, at production scale (Chapters 6 and 7), and Kata 1 in Chapter 25 is a timed exercise in the same shape.

Show a user when their account may be compromised (25 minutes, Angular, AI allowed)

Reviewers look at:

Criterion The habit
Core requirements Get something correct on screen in the first ten minutes
How do you pass information between components? Inputs down, outputs up; a container that owns data and side effects
Edge cases Empty, loading, error, unknown values, the boundary of every rule
How do you display and format dates? UTC on the wire; parse strictly; format with Intl in the user’s zone; relative time with an injectable “now”
Names, structure, comments As above

Twenty-five minutes is very little. The guide says the scenario “does not require expert-level knowledge of Angular”, and the environment is preconfigured. The candidates who do well are the ones who do not have to think about how to pass data to a child component or how to format a date in a zone, because they have done it twenty times. Chapters 17 and 18 exist so that you have.

1.3 Ten minutes in Qualified

Do what the guide says: open the Qualified practice environment before the real thing and spend ten minutes in it. Specifically, find out:

  • how to run the tests, and how long a run takes;
  • where console output appears (you will want Console.WriteLine or console.log when a test fails mysteriously);
  • whether you can add a test file or only edit the provided ones;
  • which language version and framework version it runs. Look for the Angular version in particular: if it predates Angular 17 you will be writing *ngIf and @Input() rather than @if and input(). Appendix C translates everything in this book into the older syntax.

1.4 A timetable for each scenario

Timers make people skip the parts that earn marks. Decide your timetable in advance and keep to it.

Debugging (35 min): 3 read the report and write down what you know and don’t · 7 reproduce · 12 investigate and fix · 3 regression test · 10 write-ups (engineer + non-engineer). If you have not found the cause at minute 22, stop and write up what you have ruled out: a clear record of an unfinished investigation is worth more than a silent half-fix.

Authorisation (40 min): 5 read, restate requirements, list edge cases in a comment · 20 implement · 10 add tests for each edge case · 5 tidy names and write the “Decisions” comment.

Angular (25 min): 3 read and sketch the component tree · 10 get the data on screen, correctly · 7 edge cases (empty, unknown, date formatting) · 5 names, comments, AI citation.

1.5 What this chapter asks you to do

Nothing yet, except decide when you will sit the test and work backwards. The rest of the book is built so that by test day each of the habits above is something you have done, not something you have read about.

Chapter 2 · The Sentinel Domain

Before you can model a domain you must understand it. This chapter has almost no code. It is the chapter the others depend on, because every decision in the code is downstream of the vocabulary set here.

2.1 What Sentinel is

Sentinel is the internal portal of a mid-sized company. Employees sign in to it to reach reports, billing, the support desk and administration screens. It answers two questions, constantly:

  1. May this person open this page? — the access half.
  2. Is this person really this person? — the account security half.

Each half has a rule engine in the domain layer. PageAccessEvaluator answers the first (Chapter 7); CompromiseDetector answers the second (Chapter 8). Everything else in the system exists to feed those two engines data and to show their verdicts to people.

2.2 The actors

Actor What they do in Sentinel
Employee Signs in, uses the pages their roles allow, checks their own account security
Administrator Manages users, roles and pages; investigates “why can’t X see Y?”
Auditor May look at users and every report; may change nothing
Support agent Fields tickets from employees; forwards bugs to engineering
Identity provider An external system that performs the actual sign-in and reports each attempt to Sentinel

The last actor is important and easily forgotten: Sentinel does not check passwords. It records sign-in attempts reported by an identity provider (Azure AD, Okta, Keycloak…) and analyses them. In development, you play the identity provider with the .http file or curl.

2.3 The vocabulary

Permission. A named capability, written as dot-separated lower-case segments: reports.finance, admin.users.manage. A grant may end in a wildcard: reports.* covers every permission beneath reports, and * covers everything. A page always requires a concrete permission, never a wildcard.

Role. A named bundle of permissions: Finance Manager grants reports.view, reports.finance, reports.finance.* and billing.*.

User. A person, with an email address, a display name, an IANA time zone such as Africa/Lagos, a status (Active or Suspended), a set of roles, and optional per-user overrides: a direct Allow or Deny of one permission.

Page. A screen in the portal, identified by its path (/reports/finance). Pages form a tree: every page except the roots has a parent. A page may require a permission, require only that you are signed in, or be public.

Sign-in attempt. One attempt to sign in, successful or failed, with its time (UTC), IP address, approximate location and device.

Finding. One reason to think an account may be compromised: a brute-force burst, impossible travel, a new country, a new device. Each has a severity (Low, Medium, High).

Assessment. The findings for one account and the worst of their severities, the risk level.

Acknowledgement. The user’s “that was me” on a finding. An acknowledged finding no longer raises the risk level.

2.4 The access rules

These are the rules the business agreed. They are written as numbered statements because that is how you should write rules you are about to implement in a timed test, too.

  1. A public page may be opened by anyone, signed in or not.
  2. Nobody else may open anything unless signed in and active. A suspended user sees public pages only.
  3. A page may be opened only if its parent may be opened. You cannot reach a room through a locked door.
  4. A page with no required permission may be opened by any active user (subject to rule 3).
  5. A page that requires a permission may be opened if any of the user’s grants covers it (rule 7), and
  6. no deny covers it. An explicit deny beats every allow, from any role.
  7. A grant x covers x. A grant x.* covers anything that starts x., at any depth, but not x itself. A grant * covers everything.
  8. Bad data fails closed: a page whose parent does not exist, or whose ancestry loops back on itself, may not be opened by anyone.

Rule 8 is the one people forget, and the one a reviewer looks for. Data that “cannot happen” happens: an import goes wrong, a test builds a tree by hand, a future cache serves a stale parent. The access rules must never throw and must never let someone in by accident.

2.5 The compromise rules

Agreed with the security team, with thresholds that can be tuned:

Finding Rule Severity
Brute force At least 5 failed attempts within any 15-minute window Medium; High if a success follows within the window
Impossible travel Two consecutive successful sign-ins more than 500 km apart, implying a speed above 900 km/h High
New country A successful sign-in from a country this user has never signed in from successfully Medium
New device A successful sign-in from a device this user has never used Low

And the conditions around them:

  • Findings are reported only for the last 30 days, but the previous 90 days count as “seen before”.
  • A user’s first ever successful sign-in is never “new” anything; there is nothing to compare it with.
  • A failed sign-in from a new country does not make that country “known”.
  • Attempts after now (clock skew upstream) are ignored.
  • The risk level is the highest severity among unacknowledged findings. Medium and above are “compromise suspected”: the UI interrupts the user.

2.6 The people in the seed data

Every developer database is seeded with eight people, each of whom tells one story. You will meet them throughout the book; this table is worth a bookmark.

User Role Zone Story Expected risk
Ada Okafor Administrator Africa/Lagos Ordinary; one new phone Low
Bola Adeyemi Finance Manager Africa/Lagos Lagos, then London 40 minutes later High
Chen Wei Operations Asia/Singapore 8 failures from Frankfurt in 9 minutes, none succeeded Medium
Dana Smith Support Agent America/New_York A real trip to London on a new laptop Medium
Emeka Nwosu Finance Manager + deny reports.finance.export Europe/London A contractor None
Femi Bello Auditor Africa/Lagos Reads users, changes nothing None
Grace Eze Support Agent, suspended Africa/Lagos Left the company None
Tunde Bakare Operations Africa/Lagos 500+ scripted sign-ins; then a successful attack from Amsterdam High

2.7 What we are deliberately not building

Real identity platforms do much more. Sentinel does not authenticate passwords, send email, lock accounts, or keep an audit log. It uses a development-only authentication scheme (Chapter 12). The pages behind the menu (reports, billing) are placeholders. Every one of those omissions is a place where the book would grow without teaching anything new about the three scenarios.

Chapter 3 · The Architecture

3.1 The dependency rule

Clean Architecture is usually taught as concentric circles, which is memorable and nearly useless, because a picture does not tell you what to do on a Tuesday afternoon. It reduces to one mechanical rule:

Source code dependencies point only inwards. An inner layer never names a type defined in an outer layer.

Everything else (ports, adapters, dependency inversion) is technique for obeying that rule when control has to flow the other way. Sentinel has four production layers and a contracts assembly:

          ┌──────────────────────────────┐
          │  Sentinel.Api                │  Minimal API endpoints, auth, composition root
          └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                         │ depends on
          ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
          │  Sentinel.Infrastructure     │  EF Core, SQL Server, clock, geolocation, seeding
          └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                         │ depends on
          ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
          │  Sentinel.Application        │  Commands, queries, handlers, ports, behaviours
          └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                         │ depends on
          ┌──────────────▼───────────────┐
          │  Sentinel.Domain             │  Entities, value objects, the two rule engines
          └──────────────────────────────┘

  Sentinel.Contracts ──► referenced by Application and Api (DTOs only)
  client/sentinel-web ──► knows only the HTTP API and its own copies of the DTOs

Sentinel.Domain references nothing but the base class library. No EF Core, no ASP.NET, no NuGet packages at all; an architecture test (Chapter 13) fails the build if one appears.

Sentinel.Application references Domain and Contracts. It defines the ports, interfaces such as IApplicationDbContext, IClock and IGeoLocator, and contains every command, query and handler. It does not know SQL Server exists.

Sentinel.Infrastructure implements the ports: the EF Core context, the system clock, a geolocation table.

Sentinel.Api is the composition root. It references everything and is referenced by nothing.

Sentinel.Contracts is a deliberately anaemic assembly of request and response records: the wire format. The Angular client mirrors it by hand.

3.2 Why the domain has no dependencies

The two rule engines are the most valuable code in the system and the longest-lived. Every dependency you add to them is a constraint on how they can evolve and a cost on every test. PageAccessEvaluator can be unit tested with nothing but new: no database, no web host, no mocks. That is not purity for its own sake; it is why Chapter 7 has thirty tests that run in under a second.

It is also the single most transferable lesson for the second scenario. In a 40-minute test, write the rules as a pure function of their inputs, then test that function. Do not let I/O anywhere near it.

3.3 CQRS, and what it means here

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) is often described as needing two databases and an event bus. It needs neither. Its essence is:

The model you use to change state need not be the model you use to read it.

Sentinel’s version, sometimes called “CQRS-lite”, is the right default for a system of this size:

  • Commands load an aggregate with change tracking, call a method on it, and save. AssignRoleCommandHandler loads a User, calls user.AssignRole(roleId, now), and lets the aggregate decide whether that is allowed. The handler contains almost no logic.
  • Queries never modify anything. They read with AsNoTracking() and shape a DTO for the screen. GetAccountSecurityStatusQueryHandler loads history, runs the detector, and returns exactly what the page needs.

Both kinds are messages (record types) dispatched to exactly one handler. That uniformity is what lets cross-cutting behaviour (validation, logging) be written once (Chapter 9).

3.4 Vertical slices inside the layers

Inside Application, code is organised by feature, then use case, never by technical kind:

src/Sentinel.Application/
├── Abstractions/        Messaging/, Validation/, Ports/
├── Behaviors/           ValidationBehavior, LoggingBehavior
├── Access/HasPermission/
├── Pages/
│   ├── CheckPageAccess/     CheckPageAccessQuery.cs, CheckPageAccessQueryHandler.cs
│   ├── GetNavigation/
│   ├── GetPageAccess/
│   └── ...
├── Security/
│   ├── GetAccountSecurityStatus/
│   ├── AcknowledgeFinding/
│   └── ...
├── Roles/  └── Users/

A developer asked to change how findings are acknowledged opens one folder. The alternative, top-level Commands/, Handlers/ and Validators/ folders, scatters each use case across three places and gets worse with every feature. An architecture test (Chapter 13) enforces the folder convention.

Vertical slices and Clean Architecture are sometimes presented as rivals. They are not: the layers decide which direction dependencies point; the slices decide how code is grouped within a layer. Sentinel uses both.

3.5 SOLID, concretely

SOLID is easy to recite and hard to recognise. Here is where each principle lives in this codebase, so you can point at it in an interview.

Principle Where you can see it
Single responsibility Each handler does one use case. PageAccessEvaluator decides access; it does not load data or build menus (PageAccessMapping does that).
Open/closed Adding a use case adds a folder; nothing existing changes, because handlers and validators are discovered by AddApplication(). Adding a pipeline behaviour wraps every handler without editing any.
Liskov substitution Result<T> is usable anywhere a Result is expected; ValidationError anywhere an Error is. The kata tests run one test class against two implementations of the same interface.
Interface segregation IClock has one member. IGeoLocator has one. The Angular Session exposes read-only signals, not its writable state.
Dependency inversion Application owns IApplicationDbContext; Infrastructure implements it. The arrow of the source dependency points inwards even though control flows outwards.

3.6 The dispatcher, and a note on MediatR

Most CQRS samples in .NET reach for MediatR. Since version 13 MediatR is commercially licensed above a revenue threshold. We write our own dispatcher instead: about sixty lines, no licensing question, and writing it teaches exactly what MediatR does (Chapter 9). Swapping to MediatR or Wolverine later is mechanical.

3.7 A note on repositories

We do not use the repository pattern. DbContext already is a unit of work with repositories hanging off it; wrapping it yields either a leaky abstraction that exposes IQueryable (and abstracts nothing) or a growing interface with a method per query. The Application layer depends on IApplicationDbContext, an interface it owns, which satisfies the dependency rule while keeping LINQ.

3.8 What is not here, and when it would be

Domain events. Nothing in Sentinel reacts to a change in another aggregate yet. When something does (say, “suspending a user acknowledges nothing and emails security”), raise an event from the aggregate and dispatch it after SaveChanges. Until then, an event bus with no subscribers is ceremony.

A read model. The page access queries load the whole page tree on every call. With tens of pages that costs microseconds. With tens of thousands, cache the tree and invalidate it when a page changes. Measure first.

Part II · The Back End

Chapter 4 · Environment and Solution Setup

4.1 What to install

  • .NET 10 SDK (10.0.3xx or later). Check with dotnet --list-sdks.
  • Visual Studio 2026 with the ASP.NET and web development workload, or VS Code with C# Dev Kit, or Rider. Nothing in this book needs a particular IDE.
  • SQL Server: LocalDB (installed with Visual Studio) is enough. Any edition from 2019 works; set the connection string in src/Sentinel.Api/appsettings.json or with user secrets.
  • Node.js 22 or later (24 LTS recommended) and npm 10+, for Angular.
  • Git.
  • Optionally pandoc and Chrome or Edge, to build this book.

dotnet --list-sdks

4.3 Central build configuration

Settings every project shares go in one file at the root. MSBuild finds Directory.Build.props by walking up from each project:

Directory.Build.props 
<Project>
  <!-- Applies to every project under this folder. Keep it boring: anything
       project-specific belongs in that project's .csproj. -->
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <!-- CS1591: missing XML comment. We document intent, not every member. -->
    <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);CS1591</NoWarn>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>

TreatWarningsAsErrors is worth its occasional annoyance. A nullable warning ignored today is a NullReferenceException reported by a customer next month, and a debugging lab in this book.

Pin the SDK so that everyone builds with the same compiler:

global.json 
{
  "sdk": {
    "version": "10.0.301",
    "rollForward": "latestFeature"
  }
}

4.4 Central package management

Versions are declared once, in Directory.Packages.props; project files name packages without versions.

Directory.Packages.props 
<Project>
  <!-- Central package management: every version lives here, once. -->
  <PropertyGroup>
    <!-- Lets us pin a vulnerable transitive dependency without referencing it directly. -->
    <CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled>true</CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore" Version="10.0.13" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Relational" Version="10.0.13" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer" Version="10.0.13" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite" Version="10.0.13" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design" Version="10.0.13" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions" Version="10.0.13" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions" Version="10.0.13" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi" Version="10.0.13" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing" Version="10.0.13" />
    <!-- Transitive pin: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient brings 9.0.x, which has published advisories. -->
    <PackageVersion Include="System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs" Version="10.0.13" />
    <!-- Test tooling -->
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk" Version="17.14.1" />
    <PackageVersion Include="xunit" Version="2.9.3" />
    <PackageVersion Include="xunit.runner.visualstudio" Version="3.1.4" />
    <PackageVersion Include="coverlet.collector" Version="6.0.4" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

Note the transitive pin. Microsoft.Data.SqlClient (pulled in by the EF Core SQL Server provider) depended on a version of System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs with published advisories, and with warnings as errors the build failed with NU1903. Transitive pinning lets us raise that one package without referencing it from any project. This is a real incident from writing this book: the fix took two minutes because the error message named the package and the advisory.

Chapter 5 · Domain Building Blocks

Four small types carry the whole domain: an error, a result, an entity and an aggregate root. They are worth getting exactly right, because every other class leans on them.

5.1 Errors are values, exceptions are for bugs

There are two kinds of failure. “That email is already registered” happens every day and is part of the business. “The database connection string is null” should never happen and means the program is wrong. Mixing them, by throwing exceptions for both, makes every caller wrap every call in try/catch and guess which is which.

Sentinel’s rule: business failures are returned as Error values; exceptions are reserved for programming errors.

src/Sentinel.Domain/Common/ErrorType.cs 
namespace Sentinel.Domain.Common;

/// <summary>
/// The category of a failure. The API layer maps each category to exactly one
/// HTTP status code, so adding a member here is an API change.
/// </summary>
public enum ErrorType
{
    Validation,
    NotFound,
    Conflict,
    Forbidden
}
src/Sentinel.Domain/Common/Error.cs 
namespace Sentinel.Domain.Common;

/// <summary>
/// A failure that is part of the normal flow of the business — "that email is
/// already registered", "that role does not exist". Exceptions are reserved for
/// things that should never happen; errors are things that happen every day.
/// Not sealed: the Application layer derives a ValidationError that carries
/// one message per field.
/// </summary>
public record Error(string Code, string Message, ErrorType Type)
{
    public static Error Validation(string code, string message) => new(code, message, ErrorType.Validation);
    public static Error NotFound(string code, string message) => new(code, message, ErrorType.NotFound);
    public static Error Conflict(string code, string message) => new(code, message, ErrorType.Conflict);
    public static Error Forbidden(string code, string message) => new(code, message, ErrorType.Forbidden);

    public override string ToString() => $"{Code}: {Message}";
}

An error has a stable Code (User.DuplicateEmail) that clients and tests can rely on, a human Message, and a Type that the API maps to a status code in exactly one place (Chapter 12). The record is not sealed because the Application layer derives a ValidationError that carries one message per field.

5.2 Result: success or failure, never both

src/Sentinel.Domain/Common/Result.cs 
namespace Sentinel.Domain.Common;

/// <summary>
/// The outcome of an operation that can fail for a business reason.
/// A result is either a success or a failure, never both and never neither:
/// the constructor enforces it, so no caller has to.
/// </summary>
public class Result
{
    protected Result(bool isSuccess, Error? error)
    {
        if (isSuccess && error is not null)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("A successful result cannot carry an error.");
        if (!isSuccess && error is null)
            throw new InvalidOperationException("A failed result must carry an error.");

        IsSuccess = isSuccess;
        Error = error;
    }

    public bool IsSuccess { get; }
    public bool IsFailure => !IsSuccess;

    /// <summary>Null when <see cref="IsSuccess"/> is true.</summary>
    public Error? Error { get; }

    public static Result Success() => new(true, null);
    public static Result Failure(Error error) => new(false, error);

    public static Result<T> Success<T>(T value) => Result<T>.Success(value);
    public static Result<T> Failure<T>(Error error) => Result<T>.Failure(error);

    public static implicit operator Result(Error error) => Failure(error);
}

/// <summary>A <see cref="Result"/> that carries a value when it succeeds.</summary>
public sealed class Result<T> : Result
{
    private readonly T? _value;

    private Result(T? value, bool isSuccess, Error? error) : base(isSuccess, error) => _value = value;

    /// <summary>
    /// The value of a successful result. Reading it from a failure is a
    /// programming error, so it throws rather than returning a default.
    /// </summary>
    public T Value => IsSuccess
        ? _value!
        : throw new InvalidOperationException($"Cannot read the value of a failed result ({Error}).");

    public static Result<T> Success(T value) => new(value, true, null);
    public static new Result<T> Failure(Error error) => new(default, false, error);

    public static implicit operator Result<T>(T value) => Success(value);
    public static implicit operator Result<T>(Error error) => Failure(error);
}

Points worth noticing:

  • The constructor enforces the invariant. A Result that is a success with an error, or a failure without one, cannot be constructed, so no caller ever has to check for it.
  • Reading Value from a failure throws. Returning default would turn a forgotten if (result.IsFailure) into a silent zero or null somewhere far away.
  • The implicit conversions make handlers read naturally: return UserErrors.NotFound(id); and return user.Id; both compile in a method returning Result<Guid>.

In a 40-minute coding scenario you will not build a Result type. You will still face the decision it encodes: what does my function return when the input is bad? Decide explicitly (an empty list, null, an exception), say so in a comment, and test it.

5.3 Entities and aggregate roots

src/Sentinel.Domain/Common/Entity.cs 
namespace Sentinel.Domain.Common;

/// <summary>
/// Something with an identity that outlives changes to its attributes.
/// Two entities are the same entity when their ids are equal.
/// </summary>
public abstract class Entity
{
    protected Entity(Guid id) => Id = id;

    // For EF Core materialisation only.
    protected Entity() { }

    public Guid Id { get; protected init; }

    public override bool Equals(object? obj) =>
        obj is Entity other && other.GetType() == GetType() && other.Id == Id;

    public override int GetHashCode() => HashCode.Combine(GetType(), Id);
}

Equality by id, and by type: a User and a Role that happened to share a Guid are not equal. The protected parameterless constructor exists for EF Core only.

src/Sentinel.Domain/Common/AggregateRoot.cs 
namespace Sentinel.Domain.Common;

/// <summary>
/// The entry point to a cluster of objects that must change together.
/// Outside code holds references to the root only, and every change goes
/// through a method on the root, which is where the invariants are checked.
/// </summary>
/// <remarks>
/// There are no domain events here. Nothing in Sentinel reacts to a change
/// in another aggregate yet, and an event bus with no subscribers is
/// ceremony. Chapter 3 explains when to add one.
/// </remarks>
public abstract class AggregateRoot : Entity
{
    protected AggregateRoot(Guid id) : base(id) { }
    protected AggregateRoot() { }
}

An aggregate root is the only entry point to a cluster of objects that must change together. User is a root; UserRole and PermissionOverride live inside it and are only changed through User’s methods. That is what lets User guarantee, for example, that a role is never assigned twice.

5.4 Value objects, briefly

A value object has no identity: two EmailAddress instances with the same text are the same email. Sentinel’s value objects (EmailAddress, Permission, GeoLocation) share a pattern:

  1. A private constructor.
  2. A static Create that validates, normalises and returns a Result.
  3. Equality by value (a record, or IEquatable<T> written out).
src/Sentinel.Domain/Users/EmailAddress.cs 
using System.Net.Mail;
using Sentinel.Domain.Common;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Users;

/// <summary>
/// An email address, trimmed and lower-cased so that "Ada@Example.com" and
/// "ada@example.com " are the same person. Validation is deliberately
/// shallow: the only real test of an address is sending mail to it.
/// </summary>
public sealed record EmailAddress
{
    public const int MaxLength = 254; // RFC 5321 path limit

    private EmailAddress(string value) => Value = value;

    public string Value { get; }

    public static Result<EmailAddress> Create(string? value)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
            return UserErrors.EmailRequired;

        var normalised = value.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();

        if (normalised.Length > MaxLength)
            return UserErrors.EmailInvalid(value);

        // MailAddress accepts "Display Name <a@b>", so insist that what it
        // parsed is exactly what we were given.
        return MailAddress.TryCreate(normalised, out var parsed) && parsed.Address == normalised && normalised.Contains('.')
            ? new EmailAddress(normalised)
            : UserErrors.EmailInvalid(value);
    }

    public override string ToString() => Value;
}

The validation is deliberately shallow. The only true test of an email address is delivering mail to it; everything else is a heuristic, and a strict regex rejects real addresses. Note the comment about MailAddress.TryCreate accepting a display name: that is the kind of library behaviour you only discover by testing edge cases, and the kind of discovery worth a comment.

Chapter 6 · Users, Roles and Permissions

6.1 Permission: a value object with one interesting method

src/Sentinel.Domain/Access/Permission.cs 
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
using Sentinel.Domain.Common;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Access;

/// <summary>
/// A named capability such as <c>reports.finance</c>. Permissions are
/// dot-separated, lower-case segments. A grant may end in a wildcard:
/// <c>reports.*</c> covers every permission beneath <c>reports</c>, and
/// <c>*</c> covers everything.
/// </summary>
/// <remarks>
/// Wildcards are only meaningful on the granting side. A page *requires*
/// a concrete permission; a role may *grant* a pattern. <c>reports.*</c>
/// deliberately does not cover <c>reports</c> itself: "everything under
/// reports" is not the same claim as "the reports landing page".
/// </remarks>
public sealed partial class Permission : IEquatable<Permission>
{
    public const string Wildcard = "*";

    private Permission(string value) => Value = value;

    public string Value { get; }

    public bool IsWildcard => Value == Wildcard || Value.EndsWith(".*", StringComparison.Ordinal);

    public static Result<Permission> Create(string? value)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
            return PermissionErrors.Blank;

        var normalised = value.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();

        return normalised == Wildcard || PermissionPattern().IsMatch(normalised)
            ? new Permission(normalised)
            : PermissionErrors.Malformed(value);
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// For values already validated: seed data and database rows. Throws on
    /// bad input because bad input here is a bug, not a user mistake.
    /// </summary>
    public static Permission From(string value)
    {
        var result = Create(value);
        return result.IsSuccess
            ? result.Value
            : throw new ArgumentException(result.Error!.Message, nameof(value));
    }

    /// <summary>Does this grant (or deny) cover the <paramref name="required"/> permission?</summary>
    public bool Covers(Permission required)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(required);

        if (Value == Wildcard)
            return true;

        if (!IsWildcard)
            return Value == required.Value;

        // "reports.*" -> the prefix "reports." must start the required value.
        var prefix = Value[..^1];
        return required.Value.StartsWith(prefix, StringComparison.Ordinal);
    }

    public bool Equals(Permission? other) => other is not null && other.Value == Value;
    public override bool Equals(object? obj) => Equals(obj as Permission);
    public override int GetHashCode() => Value.GetHashCode(StringComparison.Ordinal);
    public override string ToString() => Value;

    // segment(.segment)* optionally followed by ".*"
    [GeneratedRegex(@"^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*(\.[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*)*(\.\*)?$")]
    private static partial Regex PermissionPattern();
}

public static class PermissionErrors
{
    public static readonly Error Blank =
        Error.Validation("Permission.Blank", "A permission name is required.");

    public static Error Malformed(string value) =>
        Error.Validation("Permission.Malformed",
            $"'{value}' is not a valid permission. Use dot-separated segments such as 'reports.finance' or 'reports.*'.");
}

Create normalises (trim, lower-case) and validates against one regular expression. The pattern reads: one or more segments of [a-z0-9_-], separated by dots, optionally ending in .*; or the single wildcard *. [GeneratedRegex] compiles it at build time, so there is no start-up cost and no risk of a typo surfacing only at run time.

Covers is the rule from §2.4, rule 7, and nothing else:

Grant Required Covers? Why
reports.finance reports.finance yes exact match
reports.* reports.finance.export yes any depth
reports.* reports no “everything under” ≠ “the thing itself”
reports.* reportsx.finance no the prefix includes the dot
reports.finance reports.finance.export no a concrete grant has no children
* anything yes superuser

The fourth row is the one that catches people. Implementing the wildcard as required.StartsWith("reports") would let reports.* cover reportsx. Keeping the trailing dot in the prefix (Value[..^1] drops only the *) makes the comparison segment-aware.

When a rule has a table like this, put the table in your tests as a [Theory]. PermissionTests.Covers in Chapter 13 is exactly this table.

6.2 Role

src/Sentinel.Domain/Roles/Role.cs 
using Sentinel.Domain.Access;
using Sentinel.Domain.Common;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Roles;

/// <summary>A named bundle of permissions, such as "Finance Analyst".</summary>
public sealed class Role : AggregateRoot
{
    public const int MaxNameLength = 64;

    // Not readonly: EF Core assigns a fresh list when it reads the column.
    private List<Permission> _permissions = [];

    private Role(Guid id, string name, string description) : base(id)
    {
        Name = name;
        Description = description;
    }

    // For EF Core.
    private Role() { }

    public string Name { get; private set; } = null!;
    public string Description { get; private set; } = null!;

    public IReadOnlyCollection<Permission> Permissions => _permissions.AsReadOnly();

    public static Result<Role> Create(string name, string? description = null, Guid? id = null)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(name))
            return RoleErrors.NameRequired;

        if (name.Trim().Length > MaxNameLength)
            return RoleErrors.NameTooLong;

        return new Role(id ?? Guid.CreateVersion7(), name.Trim(), description?.Trim() ?? string.Empty);
    }

    public Result Grant(Permission permission)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(permission);

        if (_permissions.Contains(permission))
            return RoleErrors.AlreadyGranted(Name, permission);

        _permissions.Add(permission);
        return Result.Success();
    }

    public Result Revoke(Permission permission)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(permission);

        return _permissions.Remove(permission)
            ? Result.Success()
            : RoleErrors.NotGranted(Name, permission);
    }
}

public static class RoleErrors
{
    public static readonly Error NameRequired =
        Error.Validation("Role.NameRequired", "A role name is required.");

    public static readonly Error NameTooLong =
        Error.Validation("Role.NameTooLong", $"A role name cannot exceed {Role.MaxNameLength} characters.");

    public static Error DuplicateName(string name) =>
        Error.Conflict("Role.DuplicateName", $"A role named '{name}' already exists.");

    public static Error NotFound(Guid id) =>
        Error.NotFound("Role.NotFound", $"Role {id} does not exist.");

    public static Error AlreadyGranted(string role, Permission permission) =>
        Error.Conflict("Role.AlreadyGranted", $"Role '{role}' already grants '{permission}'.");

    public static Error NotGranted(string role, Permission permission) =>
        Error.NotFound("Role.NotGranted", $"Role '{role}' does not grant '{permission}'.");
}

A role grants each permission at most once; granting twice is a Conflict, revoking something not granted is NotFound. The field _permissions is not readonly because EF Core assigns a new list when it reads the column (Chapter 11). The public Permissions property is a read-only view, so nothing outside the aggregate can add to the list behind its back.

6.3 User

src/Sentinel.Domain/Users/User.cs 
using Sentinel.Domain.Access;
using Sentinel.Domain.Common;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Users;

public enum UserStatus
{
    Active,
    Suspended
}

/// <summary>A role held by a user. Part of the <see cref="User"/> aggregate.</summary>
public sealed class UserRole
{
    internal UserRole(Guid roleId, DateTime assignedAtUtc)
    {
        RoleId = roleId;
        AssignedAtUtc = assignedAtUtc;
    }

    // For EF Core.
    private UserRole() { }

    public Guid RoleId { get; private set; }
    public DateTime AssignedAtUtc { get; private set; }
}

/// <summary>
/// A permission granted or denied to one user directly, regardless of role.
/// Denies exist for the "everyone in Finance except the contractor" case.
/// </summary>
public sealed class PermissionOverride
{
    internal PermissionOverride(Permission permission, PermissionEffect effect)
    {
        Permission = permission;
        Effect = effect;
    }

    // For EF Core.
    private PermissionOverride() { }

    public Permission Permission { get; private set; } = null!;
    public PermissionEffect Effect { get; private set; }
}

/// <summary>A person who signs in to the portal.</summary>
public sealed class User : AggregateRoot
{
    public const int MaxDisplayNameLength = 100;

    private readonly List<UserRole> _roles = [];
    private readonly List<PermissionOverride> _overrides = [];

    private User(Guid id, EmailAddress email, string displayName, string timeZoneId, DateTime createdAtUtc) : base(id)
    {
        Email = email;
        DisplayName = displayName;
        TimeZoneId = timeZoneId;
        CreatedAtUtc = createdAtUtc;
        Status = UserStatus.Active;
    }

    // For EF Core.
    private User() { }

    public EmailAddress Email { get; private set; } = null!;
    public string DisplayName { get; private set; } = null!;

    /// <summary>
    /// An IANA zone such as <c>Africa/Lagos</c>. Timestamps are stored in UTC
    /// and converted to this zone only at the moment they are shown.
    /// </summary>
    public string TimeZoneId { get; private set; } = null!;

    public UserStatus Status { get; private set; }
    public string? SuspensionReason { get; private set; }
    public DateTime CreatedAtUtc { get; private set; }

    public IReadOnlyCollection<UserRole> Roles => _roles.AsReadOnly();
    public IEnumerable<Guid> RoleIds => _roles.Select(r => r.RoleId);
    public IReadOnlyCollection<PermissionOverride> Overrides => _overrides.AsReadOnly();

    public static Result<User> Create(EmailAddress email, string displayName, string timeZoneId, DateTime nowUtc, Guid? id = null)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(email);

        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(displayName))
            return UserErrors.DisplayNameRequired;

        if (displayName.Trim().Length > MaxDisplayNameLength)
            return UserErrors.DisplayNameTooLong;

        if (!IsKnownTimeZone(timeZoneId))
            return UserErrors.UnknownTimeZone(timeZoneId);

        return new User(id ?? Guid.CreateVersion7(), email, displayName.Trim(), timeZoneId, EnsureUtc(nowUtc));
    }

    public Result AssignRole(Guid roleId, DateTime nowUtc)
    {
        if (_roles.Any(r => r.RoleId == roleId))
            return UserErrors.RoleAlreadyAssigned(roleId);

        _roles.Add(new UserRole(roleId, EnsureUtc(nowUtc)));
        return Result.Success();
    }

    public Result RevokeRole(Guid roleId)
    {
        var held = _roles.FirstOrDefault(r => r.RoleId == roleId);
        if (held is null)
            return UserErrors.RoleNotAssigned(roleId);

        _roles.Remove(held);
        return Result.Success();
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Adds or replaces the user's override for <paramref name="permission"/>.
    /// A user has at most one override per permission: allowing and denying
    /// the same thing at once has no meaning.
    /// </summary>
    public Result SetOverride(Permission permission, PermissionEffect effect)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(permission);

        _overrides.RemoveAll(o => o.Permission == permission);
        _overrides.Add(new PermissionOverride(permission, effect));
        return Result.Success();
    }

    public Result ClearOverride(Permission permission)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(permission);

        return _overrides.RemoveAll(o => o.Permission == permission) > 0
            ? Result.Success()
            : UserErrors.OverrideNotFound(permission);
    }

    public Result Suspend(string reason)
    {
        if (Status == UserStatus.Suspended)
            return UserErrors.AlreadySuspended;

        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(reason))
            return UserErrors.SuspensionReasonRequired;

        Status = UserStatus.Suspended;
        SuspensionReason = reason.Trim();
        return Result.Success();
    }

    public Result Reactivate()
    {
        if (Status == UserStatus.Active)
            return UserErrors.NotSuspended;

        Status = UserStatus.Active;
        SuspensionReason = null;
        return Result.Success();
    }

    private static bool IsKnownTimeZone(string? timeZoneId) =>
        !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(timeZoneId) && TimeZoneInfo.TryFindSystemTimeZoneById(timeZoneId, out _);

    private static DateTime EnsureUtc(DateTime value) =>
        value.Kind == DateTimeKind.Utc
            ? value
            : throw new ArgumentException("Timestamps must be UTC.", nameof(value));
}

public static class UserErrors
{
    public static readonly Error EmailRequired =
        Error.Validation("User.EmailRequired", "An email address is required.");

    public static Error EmailInvalid(string? email) =>
        Error.Validation("User.EmailInvalid", $"'{email}' is not a valid email address.");

    public static readonly Error DisplayNameRequired =
        Error.Validation("User.DisplayNameRequired", "A display name is required.");

    public static readonly Error DisplayNameTooLong =
        Error.Validation("User.DisplayNameTooLong", $"A display name cannot exceed {User.MaxDisplayNameLength} characters.");

    public static Error UnknownTimeZone(string? zone) =>
        Error.Validation("User.UnknownTimeZone", $"'{zone}' is not a recognised time zone. Use an IANA name such as 'Africa/Lagos'.");

    public static Error DuplicateEmail(EmailAddress email) =>
        Error.Conflict("User.DuplicateEmail", $"A user with email '{email}' already exists.");

    public static Error NotFound(Guid id) =>
        Error.NotFound("User.NotFound", $"User {id} does not exist.");

    public static Error RoleAlreadyAssigned(Guid roleId) =>
        Error.Conflict("User.RoleAlreadyAssigned", $"The user already holds role {roleId}.");

    public static Error RoleNotAssigned(Guid roleId) =>
        Error.NotFound("User.RoleNotAssigned", $"The user does not hold role {roleId}.");

    public static Error OverrideNotFound(Permission permission) =>
        Error.NotFound("User.OverrideNotFound", $"The user has no override for '{permission}'.");

    public static readonly Error AlreadySuspended =
        Error.Conflict("User.AlreadySuspended", "The user is already suspended.");

    public static readonly Error NotSuspended =
        Error.Conflict("User.NotSuspended", "The user is not suspended.");

    public static readonly Error SuspensionReasonRequired =
        Error.Validation("User.SuspensionReasonRequired", "A reason is required to suspend a user.");
}

Points worth studying:

  • Time zones are validated at creation with TimeZoneInfo.TryFindSystemTimeZoneById, which on .NET 6+ accepts IANA names (Africa/Lagos) on every operating system. A user with a bad zone would break every date on their security page; reject it at the door.
  • Every timestamp must be UTC. EnsureUtc throws for any other Kind, because a local time slipping into the domain is a bug, not a user error. You will see what happens when that promise breaks on the way out of the database in Chapter 22.
  • One override per permission. SetOverride replaces rather than adds: allowing and denying the same thing at once has no meaning.
  • Suspension carries a reason. Suspending twice is a conflict, not a silent success, so an administrator who thinks they are suspending an active user learns that someone else already did.

6.4 AccessSubject: flattening a user for the rules

The access rules do not need a User. They need three facts: is this person active, what do they hold, what is denied to them. AccessSubject is that, and nothing more:

src/Sentinel.Domain/Access/AccessSubject.cs 
using Sentinel.Domain.Roles;
using Sentinel.Domain.Users;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Access;

public enum SubjectStatus
{
    Anonymous,
    Active,
    Suspended
}

/// <summary>
/// Everything the access rules need to know about the person asking, and
/// nothing else. Flattening the user and their roles into this shape is what
/// lets <see cref="PageAccessEvaluator"/> stay a pure function: no database,
/// no clock, no HTTP context.
/// </summary>
public sealed class AccessSubject
{
    private AccessSubject(SubjectStatus status, IReadOnlyCollection<Permission> granted, IReadOnlyCollection<Permission> denied)
    {
        Status = status;
        Granted = granted;
        Denied = denied;
    }

    public SubjectStatus Status { get; }
    public IReadOnlyCollection<Permission> Granted { get; }
    public IReadOnlyCollection<Permission> Denied { get; }

    public static AccessSubject Anonymous { get; } = new(SubjectStatus.Anonymous, [], []);

    public static AccessSubject Create(SubjectStatus status, IEnumerable<Permission> granted, IEnumerable<Permission> denied) =>
        new(status, granted.Distinct().ToList(), denied.Distinct().ToList());

    /// <summary>
    /// Builds the subject for <paramref name="user"/>. <paramref name="roles"/> may
    /// contain roles the user does not hold (only the user's own roles count),
    /// so callers can pass every role without filtering first.
    /// </summary>
    public static AccessSubject For(User user, IEnumerable<Role> roles)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(user);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(roles);

        var heldRoleIds = user.RoleIds.ToHashSet();

        var granted = roles
            .Where(role => heldRoleIds.Contains(role.Id))
            .SelectMany(role => role.Permissions)
            .Concat(user.Overrides.Where(o => o.Effect == PermissionEffect.Allow).Select(o => o.Permission));

        var denied = user.Overrides
            .Where(o => o.Effect == PermissionEffect.Deny)
            .Select(o => o.Permission);

        var status = user.Status == UserStatus.Active ? SubjectStatus.Active : SubjectStatus.Suspended;
        return Create(status, granted, denied);
    }

    public bool IsDenied(Permission required) => Denied.Any(d => d.Covers(required));

    public bool IsGranted(Permission required) => Granted.Any(g => g.Covers(required));

    /// <summary>Deny always wins over allow, whichever role the allow came from.</summary>
    public bool Has(Permission required) =>
        Status == SubjectStatus.Active && !IsDenied(required) && IsGranted(required);
}

For(user, roles) accepts every role and keeps only the user’s own. That makes the caller simpler (pass the list you have) and puts the filtering rule, the one thing that must not be got wrong, in one tested place.

Has encodes “deny wins”: it is !IsDenied && IsGranted, in that order, and it is false for anyone who is not active.

src/Sentinel.Domain/Access/PermissionEffect.cs 
namespace Sentinel.Domain.Access;

/// <summary>Whether a user-level override adds a permission or takes it away.</summary>
public enum PermissionEffect
{
    Allow,
    Deny
}

Chapter 7 · The Page Access Evaluator

This chapter is the long version of the skill test’s second scenario. Read it twice: once for the code, once for the process, because the process is what you will reproduce in 40 minutes.

7.1 The process, before any code

Step 1 — restate the requirements as a numbered list. You have seen it already: §2.4, rules 1 to 8. In the test, write that list as a comment at the top of your class before writing anything else. It costs two minutes, and it is the first thing a reviewer reads.

Step 2 — list the edge cases and decide each one. For page access:

Edge case Decision Why
Page’s parent does not exist Deny, reason OrphanedPage Fail closed
Parent cycle (/a → /b → /a) Deny pages on the cycle (CyclicHierarchy), and pages below it as ParentDenied Fail closed; no infinite loop
A page is its own parent Impossible to create (Page.Create/MoveUnder refuse) and handled if it arrives anyway Belt and braces
Two pages share an id Throw ArgumentException A programming error in the caller, not bad business data
Public page under a private parent Allow Public means public; the menu promotes it
Path with different case or a trailing slash Normalise before comparing /Admin/ and /admin are one page
Unknown path Return null “No such page” is not “denied”
Very deep tree Must not overflow or go quadratic beyond reason Memoise decisions
Empty page list Empty result Not an error

Step 3 — pick the shape. A pure function: subject and pages in, decisions out. Every decision carries a reason, because “denied” with no reason becomes a support ticket (Chapter 19 builds the screen that shows them).

Step 4 — write it, then test each decision from step 2.

7.2 The supporting types

src/Sentinel.Domain/Access/AccessReason.cs 
namespace Sentinel.Domain.Access;

/// <summary>
/// Why a page was allowed or denied. Every decision carries one, because
/// "you can't see this" without a reason is tomorrow's support ticket.
/// </summary>
public enum AccessReason
{
    // Allowed
    PublicPage,
    AuthenticatedUser,
    PermissionGranted,

    // Denied
    NotAuthenticated,
    UserSuspended,
    MissingPermission,
    ExplicitlyDenied,
    ParentDenied,
    OrphanedPage,
    CyclicHierarchy
}
src/Sentinel.Domain/Access/PageAccessDecision.cs

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Access;

The page itself, and the path normalisation it relies on:

src/Sentinel.Domain/Pages/PagePath.cs 
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Pages;

/// <summary>
/// The canonical form of a page route: leading slash, lower case, no
/// trailing slash (except the root itself), no empty segments.
/// <c>" /Admin/Users/ "</c> becomes <c>"/admin/users"</c>.
/// </summary>
public static partial class PagePath
{
    public const string Root = "/";

    /// <summary>The normalised path, or null when <paramref name="raw"/> cannot be a page path.</summary>
    public static string? TryNormalise(string? raw)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(raw))
            return null;

        var path = raw.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();

        if (!path.StartsWith('/'))
            return null;

        if (path.Length > 1)
            path = path.TrimEnd('/');

        if (path.Length == 0)
            return Root; // the input was "///"

        return path == Root || SegmentedPath().IsMatch(path) ? path : null;
    }

    /// <summary>"/admin/users" -> "/admin"; "/admin" -> "/"; "/" -> null.</summary>
    public static string? ParentOf(string normalisedPath)
    {
        if (normalisedPath == Root)
            return null;

        var lastSlash = normalisedPath.LastIndexOf('/');
        return lastSlash == 0 ? Root : normalisedPath[..lastSlash];
    }

    // One or more "/segment" where a segment is [a-z0-9-]+ and has no empty parts.
    [GeneratedRegex(@"^(/[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*)+$")]
    private static partial Regex SegmentedPath();
}
src/Sentinel.Domain/Pages/Page.cs 
using Sentinel.Domain.Access;
using Sentinel.Domain.Common;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Pages;

/// <summary>
/// A screen in the portal. Pages form a tree through <see cref="ParentId"/>;
/// the tree is the navigation menu, and it is also the access model, because
/// a child page is only reachable through its parent.
/// </summary>
public sealed class Page : AggregateRoot
{
    public const int MaxTitleLength = 100;

    private Page(Guid id, string path, string title, Guid? parentId, Permission? requiredPermission, bool isPublic, int sortOrder)
        : base(id)
    {
        Path = path;
        Title = title;
        ParentId = parentId;
        RequiredPermission = requiredPermission;
        IsPublic = isPublic;
        SortOrder = sortOrder;
    }

    // For EF Core.
    private Page() { }

    /// <summary>Always normalised. See <see cref="PagePath"/>.</summary>
    public string Path { get; private set; } = null!;

    public string Title { get; private set; } = null!;

    public Guid? ParentId { get; private set; }

    /// <summary>Null means "any signed-in user"; it does not mean "anyone".</summary>
    public Permission? RequiredPermission { get; private set; }

    /// <summary>Visible without signing in. A public page cannot also require a permission.</summary>
    public bool IsPublic { get; private set; }

    public int SortOrder { get; private set; }

    public static Result<Page> Create(
        string path,
        string title,
        Guid? parentId = null,
        Permission? requiredPermission = null,
        bool isPublic = false,
        int sortOrder = 0,
        Guid? id = null)
    {
        var normalisedPath = PagePath.TryNormalise(path);
        if (normalisedPath is null)
            return PageErrors.InvalidPath(path);

        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title))
            return PageErrors.TitleRequired;

        if (title.Trim().Length > MaxTitleLength)
            return PageErrors.TitleTooLong;

        if (isPublic && requiredPermission is not null)
            return PageErrors.PublicPageWithPermission;

        var pageId = id ?? Guid.CreateVersion7();
        if (parentId == pageId)
            return PageErrors.OwnParent;

        return new Page(pageId, normalisedPath, title.Trim(), parentId, requiredPermission, isPublic, sortOrder);
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Re-parents the page. Only the trivial cycle (a page under itself) is
    /// caught here; longer cycles need the whole tree, so the evaluator
    /// treats them as corrupt data rather than trusting this method alone.
    /// </summary>
    public Result MoveUnder(Guid? parentId)
    {
        if (parentId == Id)
            return PageErrors.OwnParent;

        ParentId = parentId;
        return Result.Success();
    }

    public Result RequirePermission(Permission? permission)
    {
        if (IsPublic && permission is not null)
            return PageErrors.PublicPageWithPermission;

        RequiredPermission = permission;
        return Result.Success();
    }
}

public static class PageErrors
{
    public static Error InvalidPath(string? path) =>
        Error.Validation("Page.InvalidPath", $"'{path}' is not a valid page path. Paths look like '/reports/finance'.");

    public static readonly Error TitleRequired =
        Error.Validation("Page.TitleRequired", "A page title is required.");

    public static readonly Error TitleTooLong =
        Error.Validation("Page.TitleTooLong", $"A page title cannot exceed {Page.MaxTitleLength} characters.");

    public static readonly Error PublicPageWithPermission =
        Error.Validation("Page.PublicPageWithPermission", "A public page cannot require a permission.");

    public static readonly Error OwnParent =
        Error.Validation("Page.OwnParent", "A page cannot be its own parent.");

    public static Error DuplicatePath(string path) =>
        Error.Conflict("Page.DuplicatePath", $"A page already exists at '{path}'.");

    public static Error ParentNotFound(Guid parentId) =>
        Error.NotFound("Page.ParentNotFound", $"Parent page {parentId} does not exist.");

    public static Error NotFound(string path) =>
        Error.NotFound("Page.NotFound", $"No page exists at '{path}'.");
}

7.3 The evaluator

src/Sentinel.Domain/Access/PageAccessEvaluator.cs 
using Sentinel.Domain.Pages;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Access;

/// <summary>
/// Decides which pages a subject may open. The rules, in the order they apply:
/// <list type="number">
///   <item>A page that is part of a parent cycle is denied (the data is corrupt; fail closed).</item>
///   <item>A public page is allowed for everyone, signed in or not.</item>
///   <item>Anonymous and suspended subjects are denied everything else.</item>
///   <item>A page whose parent is missing is denied (fail closed).</item>
///   <item>A page whose parent is denied is denied: you cannot reach a room through a locked door.</item>
///   <item>A page with no required permission is allowed for any active user.</item>
///   <item>An explicit deny covering the required permission wins.</item>
///   <item>Otherwise the page is allowed if any grant covers the required permission.</item>
/// </list>
/// </summary>
/// <remarks>
/// The evaluator is a pure function of its inputs. It never throws on bad
/// data from the database (orphans and cycles become denials with a reason)
/// because a navigation menu that crashes is worse than one that hides a page.
/// </remarks>
public sealed class PageAccessEvaluator
{
    private readonly AccessSubject _subject;
    private readonly Dictionary<Guid, Page> _pagesById = [];
    private readonly Dictionary<Guid, PageAccessDecision> _decisions = [];

    private PageAccessEvaluator(AccessSubject subject, IEnumerable<Page> pages)
    {
        _subject = subject;
        foreach (var page in pages)
        {
            if (!_pagesById.TryAdd(page.Id, page))
                throw new ArgumentException($"Page id {page.Id} appears more than once.", nameof(pages));
        }
    }

    /// <summary>One decision per page, in the order the pages were supplied.</summary>
    public static IReadOnlyList<PageAccessDecision> EvaluateAll(AccessSubject subject, IEnumerable<Page> pages)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(subject);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(pages);

        var pageList = pages.ToList();
        var evaluator = new PageAccessEvaluator(subject, pageList);
        return pageList.Select(evaluator.Decide).ToList();
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// The decision for the page at <paramref name="path"/>, or null when no
    /// such page exists. Paths are compared after normalisation, so
    /// <c>/Admin/Users/</c> and <c>/admin/users</c> are the same page.
    /// </summary>
    public static PageAccessDecision? EvaluatePath(AccessSubject subject, IEnumerable<Page> pages, string path)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(subject);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(pages);

        var normalised = PagePath.TryNormalise(path);
        if (normalised is null)
            return null;

        var pageList = pages.ToList();
        var target = pageList.FirstOrDefault(p => p.Path == normalised);
        return target is null ? null : new PageAccessEvaluator(subject, pageList).Decide(target);
    }

    private PageAccessDecision Decide(Page page)
    {
        if (_decisions.TryGetValue(page.Id, out var known))
            return known;

        var decision = DecideUncached(page);
        _decisions[page.Id] = decision;
        return decision;
    }

    private PageAccessDecision DecideUncached(Page page)
    {
        if (IsOnCycle(page))
            return Deny(page, AccessReason.CyclicHierarchy);

        if (page.IsPublic)
            return Allow(page, AccessReason.PublicPage);

        switch (_subject.Status)
        {
            case SubjectStatus.Anonymous: return Deny(page, AccessReason.NotAuthenticated);
            case SubjectStatus.Suspended: return Deny(page, AccessReason.UserSuspended);
        }

        if (page.ParentId is { } parentId)
        {
            if (!_pagesById.TryGetValue(parentId, out var parent))
                return Deny(page, AccessReason.OrphanedPage);

            // Safe to recurse: this page is not on a cycle, so walking up
            // either reaches a root or reaches a page that *is* on a cycle,
            // which returns above without recursing further.
            if (!Decide(parent).IsAllowed)
                return Deny(page, AccessReason.ParentDenied);
        }

        if (page.RequiredPermission is not { } required)
            return Allow(page, AccessReason.AuthenticatedUser);

        if (_subject.IsDenied(required))
            return Deny(page, AccessReason.ExplicitlyDenied);

        return _subject.IsGranted(required)
            ? Allow(page, AccessReason.PermissionGranted)
            : Deny(page, AccessReason.MissingPermission);
    }

    /// <summary>True when following parents from <paramref name="page"/> leads back to it.</summary>
    private bool IsOnCycle(Page page)
    {
        var seen = new HashSet<Guid>();
        var current = page;

        while (current.ParentId is { } parentId && _pagesById.TryGetValue(parentId, out var parent))
        {
            if (parent.Id == page.Id)
                return true;

            // A cycle further up that does not include this page: the page
            // hangs below the cycle rather than sitting on it. ParentDenied
            // will deal with it when its ancestors are decided.
            if (!seen.Add(parent.Id))
                return false;

            current = parent;
        }

        return false;
    }

    private static PageAccessDecision Allow(Page page, AccessReason reason) => new(page, true, reason);
    private static PageAccessDecision Deny(Page page, AccessReason reason) => new(page, false, reason);
}

Read DecideUncached from top to bottom and compare it with the rules in §2.4. They are in the same order. That is not an accident; it is the cheapest way to make a reviewer trust your code.

Why memoise?

Decide caches each decision in _decisions. Without the cache, deciding every page in a tree means deciding each ancestor again for every descendant: a ten-level-deep branch decides its root ten times. With it, each page is decided once. The test A_very_deep_tree_does_not_overflow_the_stack builds a 2,000-level chain to prove the recursion depth is fine for any realistic menu.

Why is recursion safe here?

Recursion over user data is a classic way to hang a server: a cycle in the data becomes infinite recursion. The evaluator checks IsOnCycle(page) before recursing into the parent. If the page is on a cycle it returns immediately. If it is not, walking up must reach either a root or a page that is on a cycle, and that page returns without recursing. Either way the recursion terminates. The comment in the code says exactly this, because the next reader will wonder.

Why does IsOnCycle distinguish “on” from “below”?

Given /a → /b → /a and /c → /a, page /c is not on the cycle, it hangs below it. Reporting /c as CyclicHierarchy would send whoever investigates to the wrong page. Reporting it as ParentDenied points at its parent, which points at the cycle. Good reasons lead you to the cause.

Why throw for duplicate ids but not for orphans?

An orphan is bad data: it came from the database and the evaluator must cope. Duplicate ids mean the caller built a wrong list, which is a bug in our code. Bugs should be loud; data problems should be safe.

7.4 The tests

The test data builders keep each test focused on what is different about it:

tests/Sentinel.Domain.Tests/TestData.cs 
using Sentinel.Domain.Access;
using Sentinel.Domain.Pages;
using Sentinel.Domain.Security;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Tests;

/// <summary>Small, readable builders. A test should say what is different about its data, and nothing else.</summary>
internal static class Places
{
    public static readonly GeoLocation Lagos = GeoLocation.Create("NG", "Lagos", 6.5244, 3.3792);
    public static readonly GeoLocation Ikeja = GeoLocation.Create("NG", "Ikeja", 6.6018, 3.3515); // ~9 km from Lagos
    public static readonly GeoLocation Abuja = GeoLocation.Create("NG", "Abuja", 9.0765, 7.3986);
    public static readonly GeoLocation London = GeoLocation.Create("GB", "London", 51.5072, -0.1276);
    public static readonly GeoLocation NewYork = GeoLocation.Create("US", "New York", 40.7128, -74.0060);
    public static readonly GeoLocation Frankfurt = GeoLocation.Create("DE", "Frankfurt", 50.1109, 8.6821);
}

internal static class Agents
{
    public const string Laptop = "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36";
    public const string Phone = "Mozilla/5.0 (iPhone; CPU iPhone OS 18_6 like Mac OS X) AppleWebKit/605.1.15 (KHTML, like Gecko) Version/18.6 Mobile/15E148 Safari/604.1";
}

/// <summary>Builds one user's sign-in history in time order, relative to a fixed "now".</summary>
internal sealed class History
{
    public static readonly DateTime Now = new(2026, 10, 25, 12, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc);

    private readonly List<SignInAttempt> _attempts = [];
    private readonly Guid _userId = Guid.NewGuid();

    public IReadOnlyList<SignInAttempt> Attempts => _attempts;

    public SignInAttempt Last => _attempts[^1];

    public History Success(DateTime atUtc, GeoLocation? where = null, string agent = Agents.Laptop) =>
        Add(atUtc, where ?? Places.Lagos, agent, succeeded: true);

    public History Failure(DateTime atUtc, GeoLocation? where = null, string agent = Agents.Laptop) =>
        Add(atUtc, where ?? Places.Lagos, agent, succeeded: false);

    /// <summary>A month of ordinary daily sign-ins from Lagos on the laptop, ending a week ago.</summary>
    public History WithOrdinaryBaseline(int days = 30)
    {
        for (var day = days + 7; day > 7; day--)
            Success(Now.AddDays(-day).AddHours(-3));
        return this;
    }

    public History Failures(DateTime startUtc, int count, TimeSpan spacing, GeoLocation? where = null)
    {
        for (var i = 0; i < count; i++)
            Failure(startUtc + spacing * i, where);
        return this;
    }

    private History Add(DateTime atUtc, GeoLocation where, string agent, bool succeeded)
    {
        _attempts.Add(SignInAttempt.Record(
            _userId, atUtc, "102.89.34.10", where, agent, succeeded,
            succeeded ? null : SignInFailureReason.WrongPassword).Value);
        return this;
    }
}

/// <summary>Builds a page tree with readable names instead of Guids.</summary>
internal sealed class PageTree
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, Page> _byPath = [];

    public IReadOnlyList<Page> Pages => _byPath.Values.ToList();

    public Page this[string path] => _byPath[path];

    public PageTree Add(string path, string? parentPath = null, string? permission = null, bool isPublic = false)
    {
        var parentId = parentPath is null ? (Guid?)null : _byPath[parentPath].Id;
        var title = path == "/" ? "Home" : path.TrimStart('/');
        var page = Page.Create(path, title, parentId,
            permission is null ? null : Permission.From(permission), isPublic).Value;
        _byPath[page.Path] = page;
        return this;
    }

    /// <summary>The standard tree most tests share: / > reports > finance > export, plus public /help.</summary>
    public static PageTree Standard() => new PageTree()
        .Add("/")
        .Add("/reports", "/", "reports.view")
        .Add("/reports/finance", "/reports", "reports.finance")
        .Add("/reports/finance/export", "/reports/finance", "reports.finance.export")
        .Add("/reports/operations", "/reports", "reports.operations")
        .Add("/account", "/")
        .Add("/help", isPublic: true);
}

internal static class Subjects
{
    public static AccessSubject Active(params string[] granted) =>
        AccessSubject.Create(SubjectStatus.Active, granted.Select(Permission.From), []);

    public static AccessSubject ActiveWithDenies(string[] granted, string[] denied) =>
        AccessSubject.Create(SubjectStatus.Active, granted.Select(Permission.From), denied.Select(Permission.From));

    public static AccessSubject Suspended(params string[] granted) =>
        AccessSubject.Create(SubjectStatus.Suspended, granted.Select(Permission.From), []);
}

And the tests themselves. Read the names first: together they are the specification.

tests/Sentinel.Domain.Tests/Access/PageAccessEvaluatorTests.cs 
using Sentinel.Domain.Access;
using Sentinel.Domain.Pages;

namespace Sentinel.Domain.Tests.Access;

public class PageAccessEvaluatorTests
{
    private static PageAccessDecision Decide(AccessSubject subject, PageTree tree, string path) =>
        PageAccessEvaluator.EvaluatePath(subject, tree.Pages, path)
        ?? throw new InvalidOperationException($"No page at {path}");

    // ---- The happy paths ----

    [Fact]
    public void Page_without_a_permission_is_allowed_for_any_active_user()
    {
        var decision = Decide(Subjects.Active(), PageTree.Standard(), "/account");

        Assert.True(decision.IsAllowed);
        Assert.Equal(AccessReason.AuthenticatedUser, decision.Reason);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Page_is_allowed_when_a_grant_covers_its_permission()
    {
        var decision = Decide(Subjects.Active("reports.view", "reports.finance"), PageTree.Standard(), "/reports/finance");

        Assert.True(decision.IsAllowed);
        Assert.Equal(AccessReason.PermissionGranted, decision.Reason);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Wildcard_grant_covers_every_page_beneath_it()
    {
        var subject = Subjects.Active("reports.view", "reports.*");

        Assert.True(Decide(subject, PageTree.Standard(), "/reports/finance").IsAllowed);
        Assert.True(Decide(subject, PageTree.Standard(), "/reports/finance/export").IsAllowed);
        Assert.True(Decide(subject, PageTree.Standard(), "/reports/operations").IsAllowed);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Wildcard_grant_does_not_cover_the_parent_permission_itself()
    {
        // A landing page that requires "reports" itself. The grant covers
        // everything beneath reports, but not reports, and the children sit
        // behind it. (In the standard tree the landing page requires
        // "reports.view", which reports.* does cover. Writing this test the
        // first time against that tree is how we learnt the difference.)
        var tree = new PageTree()
            .Add("/reports", permission: "reports")
            .Add("/reports/finance", "/reports", "reports.finance");
        var subject = Subjects.Active("reports.*");

        Assert.Equal(AccessReason.MissingPermission, Decide(subject, tree, "/reports").Reason);
        Assert.Equal(AccessReason.ParentDenied, Decide(subject, tree, "/reports/finance").Reason);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Superuser_wildcard_allows_everything()
    {
