Chapter 22 · Lab 1 — SUP-4172: “My sign-in history shows the wrong times”

Do the lab before reading past §22.1. Set a 35-minute timer, no AI.

22.1 Setting up

git switch lab/SUP-4172-sign-in-times
dotnet ef database drop --project src/Sentinel.Infrastructure -f   # fresh, reproducible data
dotnet run --project src/Sentinel.Api
# second terminal
cd client/sentinel-web; npm start

The ticket is TICKET.md at the root of the branch:

docs/labs/SUP-4172-ticket.md 
# SUP-4172 — "My sign-in history shows the wrong times"

**Lab 1 for Chapter 22.** Everything below is exactly what support forwarded.
Nothing has been investigated yet. Start a copy of
`docs/templates/investigation-log.md` before you touch the code.

---

**From:** Kemi (Customer Support, Tier 1)
**Priority:** Normal
**Customer:** Bola Adeyemi (bola.adeyemi@sentinel.dev), Finance Manager

> Hi team, customer says the times on the Account security page are wrong.
> Quote from her email: *"I always sign in at 9 when I get to the office and
> the page says 8:00. It also says I signed in from London at 8:40 on Friday.
> I have never been to London and at 8:40 I was on the bus. Is someone else
> in my account??"* She is quite worried because of the red banner. I tried it as myself and the times look fine to me?? Not sure
> if related but we deployed the "EF Core housekeeping" change on Tuesday.
> Screenshot attached (not attached).
>
> Thanks, Kemi

---

## What you have

- This branch, which reproduces the problem. Run the API and the Angular app
  as in the README and sign in as Bola.
- `git log` — the history is real; read it like an investigator.
- No access to the customer, but you can write the questions you would send.

## What a good answer contains

1. An investigation log: hypotheses, how each was tested, sources cited.
2. A fix with a regression test that fails before and passes after.
3. A write-up for engineers (`docs/templates/engineering-write-up.md`).
4. A reply Kemi can send to Bola (`docs/templates/customer-update.md`).

Time box: 35 minutes, the length of the real scenario. Then read Chapter 22.

Stop here, start your log, and work the problem. Then read on and compare.

22.2 Reading the ticket

Known Assumed Unknown
Bola says her 09:00 sign-in shows as 08:00 That she signs in at 09:00 Lagos time Bola’s computer’s time zone
The page shows a London sign-in she denies That the two observations have the same cause Whether she was in London
Kemi’s own times “look fine” That Kemi’s account has the same kind of data Kemi’s time zone (London? UTC?)
An “EF Core housekeeping” change went out on Tuesday That it is related What that change touched

Two observations are bundled into one ticket, and they must be separated:

  1. The times are an hour early. A display problem.
  2. A sign-in from London she did not make. Possibly a real compromise, possibly a symptom of (1). Do not dismiss it: if it is real, it is the more urgent of the two.

Questions for Bola, via Kemi:

  1. What time zone is your computer set to? (Settings → Time & language.)
  2. Is it every sign-in that looks an hour early, or only some?
  3. Were you anywhere outside Nigeria last Friday, or using a VPN?

The fact that “Kemi’s times look fine” is the most useful sentence in the ticket. An off-by-one-hour error that appears for one person and not another smells of time zones, and Lagos is UTC+1.

22.3 Reproducing

Sign in as Bola. The page shows her ordinary Lagos sign-in at 08:00. The seed data puts it at 09:00 Lagos time, which is 08:00 UTC. So the page is showing the UTC wall-clock time and labelling it as Lagos.

Go one level down. Is the server wrong, or the browser?

curl -s http://localhost:5080/api/me/security -H "X-Demo-User: bola.adeyemi@sentinel.dev"
"assessedAtUtc":"2026-10-25T16:35:41.5652577Z",
...
"occurredAtUtc":"2026-10-23T08:00:00",

There it is, and it is worth slowing down to see it: assessedAtUtc ends in Z, and occurredAtUtc does not. Both are DateTime properties on the same DTO. One has a zone designator and one does not.

22.4 Hypotheses

# Hypothesis Cheapest test Result
H1 The seed data is wrong Query the database directly Ruled out: SignInAttempts.OccurredAtUtc is 08:00 (UTC, correct)
H2 The client formats in the wrong zone Call formatInZone('2026-10-23T08:00:00Z', 'Africa/Lagos') Ruled out: returns 09:00
H3 The client parses a zone-less string as local time new Date('2026-10-23T08:00:00').toISOString() in a Lagos browser Confirmed: 07:00:00.000Z, one hour early
H4 The server sends some timestamps without Z Compare the two fields in the raw JSON Confirmed: only values read from the database lack Z

H3 explains the symptom; H4 explains H3. Why do values from the database lack the Z while assessedAtUtc (from IClock) has it?

System.Text.Json writes a DateTime according to its Kind: Utc gets a Z, Local gets an offset, and Unspecified gets nothing. A value created by DateTime.UtcNow has Kind = Utc. A value read from a SQL Server datetime2 column has Kind = Unspecified, because the column has no notion of a zone. Something used to stamp Utc on values read from the database, and now does not.

22.5 Finding the change

The ticket mentions an “EF Core housekeeping” deploy. The history agrees:

git log --oneline -5
git show HEAD~1 --stat
git show HEAD~1 -- src/Sentinel.Infrastructure/Persistence/SentinelDbContext.cs
-    protected override void ConfigureConventions(ModelConfigurationBuilder configurationBuilder)
-    {
-        configurationBuilder.Properties<DateTime>().HaveConversion<UtcDateTimeConverter>();
-    }

The convention looked redundant (“datetime2 already round-trips the value”) and it was removed. It round-trips the value; it never round-tripped the kind. UtcDateTimeConverter.cs is still in the repository, now referenced by nothing, which is itself a clue worth noticing in any investigation: unused code is often the ghost of a removed fix.

The same commit simplified the client’s parser to new Date(value), which is why the server’s change became a visible symptom instead of an error.

Sources consulted (cite these in your log):

  • Microsoft Learn, DateTime.Kind and DateTime and DateTimeOffset in System.Text.Json: serialisation depends on Kind.
  • Microsoft Learn, EF Core Value Conversions: ConfigureConventions with HaveConversion applies a converter to every property of a type.
  • MDN, Date.parse(): date-time strings without an offset are interpreted as local time.

22.6 The regression tests, then the fix

Write the tests first and watch them fail on the lab branch. At the wire:

[Fact]
public async Task Every_timestamp_on_the_wire_is_utc_with_a_z()
{
    var json = await factory.ClientFor(Dana).GetStringAsync("/api/me/security");

    var timestamps = TimestampProperty().Matches(json).Select(m => m.Groups["value"].Value).ToList();

    Assert.NotEmpty(timestamps);
    Assert.All(timestamps, t => Assert.EndsWith("Z", t));
}

And at the persistence boundary, closer to the cause:

[Fact]
public async Task Sign_in_times_come_back_from_the_database_as_utc()
{
    await using var host = await TestHost.CreateAsync(seed: true);

    var status = (await host.Send(new GetAccountSecurityStatusQuery(await host.UserIdAsync("ada.okafor@sentinel.dev")))).Value;

    Assert.All(status.RecentSignIns, s => Assert.Equal(DateTimeKind.Utc, s.OccurredAtUtc.Kind));
}

Both fail. Restore the convention (the fix, as it stands on main):

src/Sentinel.Infrastructure/Persistence/SentinelDbContext.cs 
using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore;
using Sentinel.Application.Abstractions.Ports;
using Sentinel.Domain.Pages;
using Sentinel.Domain.Roles;
using Sentinel.Domain.Security;
using Sentinel.Domain.Users;
using Sentinel.Infrastructure.Persistence.Converters;

namespace Sentinel.Infrastructure.Persistence;

public sealed class SentinelDbContext(DbContextOptions<SentinelDbContext> options)
    : DbContext(options), IApplicationDbContext
{
    public DbSet<User> Users => Set<User>();
    public DbSet<Role> Roles => Set<Role>();
    public DbSet<Page> Pages => Set<Page>();
    public DbSet<SignInAttempt> SignInAttempts => Set<SignInAttempt>();
    public DbSet<FindingAcknowledgement> FindingAcknowledgements => Set<FindingAcknowledgement>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder modelBuilder) =>
        modelBuilder.ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly(typeof(SentinelDbContext).Assembly);

    protected override void ConfigureConventions(ModelConfigurationBuilder configurationBuilder)
    {
        // Every DateTime in this model is UTC. SQL Server's datetime2 has no
        // notion of a zone, so without this line every value read back has
        // DateTimeKind.Unspecified, serialises without its 'Z', and is then
        // read by every browser on earth as local time. Chapter 22 is the
        // post-mortem of deleting this line.
        configurationBuilder.Properties<DateTime>().HaveConversion<UtcDateTimeConverter>();
    }
}

Both pass. Then defence in depth on the client: a browser that receives a zone-less timestamp should say so rather than guess. That is the strict parseApiTimestamp from Chapter 18, with its own test:

it('refuses a timestamp with no zone instead of guessing local time', () => {
  const error = vi.spyOn(console, 'error').mockImplementation(() => undefined);

  expect(parseApiTimestamp('2026-10-24T08:00:00')).toBeNull();
  expect(error).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();

  error.mockRestore();
});

Is the client change part of the fix or scope creep? Argue it in your write-up either way; what matters is that you made the choice on purpose. The argument for it: the server bug was invisible for days because the client silently “handled” bad data. A client that refuses bad data turns the next such bug into an error on first use.

22.7 And the London sign-in?

With the times fixed, Bola’s history shows Lagos at 09:00 and London at 09:40, both successful, from a Windows laptop and an iPhone respectively. That is a genuine impossible travel finding. The display bug did not create it; it only made it look stranger. Your reply to support must say both things clearly: the times were wrong, we’ve fixed that; separately, the London sign-in is real and Bola should change her password now. Merging them into “it was a bug, all fine” would be the most harmful possible outcome of this ticket.

22.8 A follow-up the investigation uncovered

While reproducing, Sentinel.http showed that POST /api/sign-ins with a zone-less occurredAt is accepted and interpreted as server-local time. On a server in Lagos, 09:00 becomes 08:00Z; on a server in UTC, it stays 09:00Z. The contract says a zone is required. Record it as a follow-up (reject zone-less timestamps with a 400, via a custom JsonConverter<DateTimeOffset>), not as part of today’s fix. Knowing what not to fix in an incident is part of the skill.

22.9 The write-ups

The engineer write-up and the customer reply for this lab are in Chapter 24, as worked examples.

Chapter 23 · Lab 2 — SUP-4219: “Security page says all clear, but I got a lockout email”

Do the lab first. 35 minutes, no AI.

git switch lab/SUP-4219-all-clear
dotnet ef database drop --project src/Sentinel.Infrastructure -f
dotnet run --project src/Sentinel.Api
docs/labs/SUP-4219-ticket.md 
# SUP-4219 — "Security page says all clear, but I got a lockout email"

**Lab 2 for Chapter 23.** Exactly what support forwarded; nothing has been
investigated. Start a copy of `docs/templates/investigation-log.md` first.

---

**From:** Ifeanyi (Customer Support, Tier 2)
**Priority:** High
**Customer:** Tunde Bakare (tunde.bakare@sentinel.dev), Operations

> Tunde got the "unusual sign-in activity" email from the identity provider
> yesterday evening and someone in his team says they saw a login from
> Amsterdam. But when he opens Account security it's green, "No suspicious
> activity". I checked two other users who were in the same phishing
> campaign (Chen and Bola) and theirs show red/amber properly, so the
> detector seems to work?
>
> He uses the same account for his integration scripts, if that matters.
> Can someone look urgently, we don't know if the account is compromised.

---

## What you have

- This branch, which reproduces the problem (sign in as Tunde).
- The API, the database, and the logs (`LoggingBehavior` writes one line per request).
- `src/Sentinel.Api/Sentinel.http` for poking the API directly.

## What a good answer contains

1. An investigation log with hypotheses ruled in and out, and sources cited.
2. The fix, with a regression test that fails on this branch and passes after.
3. An answer to the question support actually asked: *is Tunde's account compromised?*
4. A write-up for engineers and a message support can send to Tunde.

Time box: 35 minutes. Then read Chapter 23.

23.1 Reading the ticket

Known Assumed Unknown
The identity provider emailed Tunde about unusual activity That the email was about real activity When exactly
A colleague “saw a login from Amsterdam” That it is in Sentinel’s data Where they saw it
Tunde’s page is green That green means “no findings” —
Chen’s and Bola’s pages work That the detector is fine What is different about Tunde
Tunde runs integration scripts on his account That it does not matter —

The support agent has done something valuable: a comparison. Two other users in the same campaign show findings, so “the detector is broken” is unlikely. The question becomes what is different about Tunde? and the ticket answers it in passing: integration scripts.

Support’s real question is not “why is the page green?” but “is Tunde’s account compromised?” Answer that first, whatever the code does.

23.2 Reproducing, and the first clue

curl -s http://localhost:5080/api/me/security -H "X-Demo-User: tunde.bakare@sentinel.dev"
{"riskLevel":"None","isCompromiseSuspected":false, ... "recentSignIns":[{"occurredAtUtc":"2026-10-18T23:37:33Z", ...

The risk is None, as reported. But look at recentSignIns[0]: the “most recent” sign-in is a week old, and Tunde’s scripts sign in every four hours. The page is not looking at recent history at all.

Check the data directly, to separate “the data is missing” from “the code is not reading it”:

SELECT COUNT(*), MIN(OccurredAtUtc), MAX(OccurredAtUtc)
FROM SignInAttempts a JOIN Users u ON u.Id = a.UserId
WHERE u.Email = 'tunde.bakare@sentinel.dev';
-- about 550 rows, from 90 days ago to a few hours ago

SELECT OccurredAtUtc, Succeeded, IpAddress FROM SignInAttempts a JOIN Users u ON u.Id = a.UserId
WHERE u.Email = 'tunde.bakare@sentinel.dev' AND a.IpAddress LIKE '145.53.%' ORDER BY OccurredAtUtc;
-- 7 failures and 1 success from Amsterdam, yesterday evening

So the attack is in the database. Answer for support, already: yes, treat Tunde’s account as compromised, a successful sign-in from Amsterdam followed seven failures. That message can go out now, before the bug is fixed.

23.3 Hypotheses

# Hypothesis Test Result
H1 The detector misses this pattern Unit test: Tunde-like history into CompromiseDetector.Assess Ruled out: High
H2 Findings are acknowledged SELECT * FROM FindingAcknowledgements for Tunde Ruled out: none
H3 The query loads the wrong attempts Log the min/max of what AccountAssessor loads Confirmed: oldest 500 of ~550

The difference between Tunde and the others: about 550 attempts in 90 days. Chen and Bola have about 45. AccountAssessor loads at most MaxHistory = 500.

23.4 The cause

var history = await db.SignInAttempts
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(a => a.UserId == userId && a.OccurredAtUtc >= since)
    .OrderBy(a => a.OccurredAtUtc)      // oldest first...
    .Take(MaxHistory)                   // ...then keep 500: the NEWEST are dropped
    .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);

OrderBy then Take keeps the oldest 500. For a user with fewer than 500 attempts the order is irrelevant, which is why every other account worked and why no test failed. The commit that introduced it had a sensible-sounding reason (“the detector walks history oldest-first, so let the database sort it”). The detector does want chronological order, and it sorts its input itself (Chapter 8 said so). The query’s order matters for one thing only: which rows survive the Take.

You can confirm without a debugger:

Console.WriteLine(query.ToQueryString());
// ... ORDER BY [s].[OccurredAtUtc] OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT @__p_1 ROWS ONLY

23.5 The regression test, then the fix

[Fact]
public async Task When_history_exceeds_the_cap_the_newest_attempts_are_assessed()
{
    await using var host = await TestHost.CreateAsync(seed: true);
    var tunde = await host.UserIdAsync("tunde.bakare@sentinel.dev");
    var total = await host.Query(db => db.SignInAttempts.CountAsync(a => a.UserId == tunde));
    Assert.True(total > AccountAssessor.MaxHistory, "The seed data must exceed the cap for this test to mean anything.");

    var status = (await host.Send(new GetAccountSecurityStatusQuery(tunde))).Value;

    Assert.Contains(status.Findings, f => f.Kind == "BruteForce" && f.Severity == "High");
}

Note the guard assertion: a test about a cap is meaningless if the data does not exceed the cap, and a future change to the seed data could make it pass vacuously. It fails on the lab branch. The fix is one word, and the comment that now sits above it on main:

src/Sentinel.Application/Security/AccountAssessor.cs (lines 40–48) 
        // Newest first, THEN take: when the ceiling bites, what we drop must
        // be the oldest baseline, never the most recent evidence. The order
        // of these two calls is the whole of Chapter 23.
        var history = await db.SignInAttempts
            .AsNoTracking()
            .Where(a => a.UserId == userId && a.OccurredAtUtc >= since)
            .OrderByDescending(a => a.OccurredAtUtc)
            .Take(MaxHistory)
            .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);

23.6 What made this bug possible

  • A truncation without a test at the limit. Every cap (Take, page size, MaxHistory) is a boundary, and boundaries get tests on both sides.
  • A comment that described the wrong concern. The order was justified by the detector’s needs, which the detector already met itself.
  • Seed data that did not exercise the cap. Tunde exists because of this incident; heavy users are real users.

23.7 Follow-ups

  • Should a user with more than 500 attempts in 90 days be assessed on 500? Dropping the oldest baseline can make an old country look “new”. Options: aggregate the baseline in SQL (distinct countries and devices) and load only the last 30 days in full. Record it; do not do it in the incident.
  • Alert on accounts whose sign-in rate looks automated: they are the ones most likely to have shared credentials.

Chapter 24 · Writing It Up for Engineers and for Everyone Else

Three of the five criteria in the debugging scenario are about writing. This chapter shows what good looks like, using both labs, and gives you the habits that produce it in ten minutes.

24.1 Two audiences, two questions

Engineers Non-engineers
Their question What broke, why, and will it happen again? Am I affected, am I safe, what do I do?
Lead with The cause, in one sentence The answer to their worry
Vocabulary Precise: file, line, type, Kind Plain: “times were shown an hour early”
Length As long as the cause needs As short as possible
Must include Why it was not caught; follow-ups What to do, if anything; how to report it again
Must not include Blame Jargon, stack traces, speculation

24.2 Worked example: SUP-4172 for engineers

SUP-4172 — Sign-in times from the database serialised without a zone and displayed one UTC offset early

Audience: engineering · Status: fixed on main · Severity: S3 (display; no data corrupted)

Summary. Commit “EF Core housekeeping” removed the ConfigureConventions override that applied UtcDateTimeConverter to every DateTime. Values read from datetime2 then had DateTimeKind.Unspecified, System.Text.Json serialised them without Z, and browsers parsed them as local time. Users east of UTC saw times early by their offset (Lagos: one hour); users west of UTC saw them late; users in UTC saw no change, which is why support could not reproduce it.

Impact. Every timestamp read from the database, on every screen, since Tuesday’s deploy. Stored data is correct; only display was wrong. Values created in memory (assessedAtUtc) were unaffected, which made the bug look intermittent.

Root cause. SentinelDbContext.ConfigureConventions was deleted as apparently redundant. datetime2 round-trips the value but not the kind. The client’s new Date(value) silently interpreted the zone-less strings.

Why it was not caught. No test asserted the wire format of timestamps or the Kind of values read back; the client accepted zone-less input.

Fix. Restored the convention. Added Every_timestamp_on_the_wire_is_utc_with_a_z (API) and Sign_in_times_come_back_from_the_database_as_utc (persistence), both red before and green after. Hardened parseApiTimestamp to reject timestamps without a designator (defence in depth: the next such bug fails loudly).

Separately: the London sign-in on Bola Adeyemi’s account is a genuine impossible-travel finding and has been passed to security.

Follow-ups. Reject zone-less occurredAt on POST /api/sign-ins (today it is read as server-local time) · add a comment to the convention so it is not “tidied” again.

References. Microsoft Learn: Value Conversions; DateTime.Kind; System.Text.Json DateTime and DateTimeOffset support. MDN: Date.parse().

Notice: the summary is three sentences and contains the whole story. The impact section says what was not affected. “Why it was not caught” describes the system, not the person who made the commit.

24.3 Worked example: SUP-4172 for the customer

Hi Bola,

What happened. A change we made on Tuesday caused the times on your Account security page to show one hour early. Your 9:00 sign-ins were displayed as 8:00. That is fixed: the times now show correctly in Lagos time.

Is your account safe? The time problem did not affect your account’s security. However, the sign-in from London last Friday is real: someone signed in to your account from London forty minutes after you signed in from Lagos. Please change your password now, and then choose This wasn’t me on that entry so our security team can follow up.

If you see anything else unusual, reply to this email with a screenshot and the time you saw it.

Thank you for reporting this: the detail that your sign-in “always” happens at 9 is what let us find the problem quickly.

Kemi, Customer Support

What makes this good: it answers her actual fear first (“is someone in my account?”), does not hide the bad news behind the good, gives one clear action, and thanks her for the specific detail that helped.

24.4 Worked example: SUP-4219, both audiences

For support (sent first, before the fix):

Ifeanyi, short answer: yes, treat Tunde’s account as compromised. Our data shows seven failed sign-ins from Amsterdam yesterday at about 21:05 UTC, followed by a successful one. Please ask him to change his password and to rotate the credentials his integration scripts use. The green status on his security page is a bug on our side, which we are fixing now; it affects only accounts with very many sign-ins.

For engineers:

SUP-4219 — Assessment loaded the oldest 500 sign-ins instead of the newest

Summary. AccountAssessor ordered history ascending before Take(500), so for users with more than 500 attempts in 90 days the most recent attempts were never assessed. A real brute-force-then-success on Tunde Bakare’s account showed as “No suspicious activity”.

Impact. Users with more than 500 sign-ins in 90 days, i.e. accounts used by automation. For them, findings from roughly the last week were invisible.

Root cause. Commit “Let the database sort sign-in history chronologically” changed OrderByDescending to OrderBy, reasoning that the detector wants oldest-first. The detector sorts its input itself; the query order only decides which rows survive Take.

Why it was not caught. No test exercised the cap; seed users had fewer than 500 attempts.

Fix. Restored OrderByDescending with a comment explaining why the order matters. Added When_history_exceeds_the_cap_the_newest_attempts_are_assessed with a guard assertion that the seed data exceeds the cap. Added a heavy-usage user to the seed data.

Follow-ups. Compute the baseline (seen countries/devices) in SQL so the cap never drops baseline either · flag automated sign-in patterns.

24.5 Habits that make this fast

  • Write the log as you go; the write-up is then mostly copying.
  • Summary first, in three sentences: what broke, why, what changed.
  • Say what you don’t know. “We have not checked other environments” is professional; silence is not.
  • Name the gap, not the person. “No test asserted…” rather than “X forgot…”.
  • For customers: answer the fear, then the facts, then the action.
  • Read the customer reply aloud. If a sentence needs an engineer to explain it, rewrite it.

24.6 The templates

docs/templates/engineering-write-up.md 
# <ticket id> — <precise technical title>

**Audience:** engineers. **Status:** fixed in <commit/branch> · **Severity:** <S1–S4>

## Summary

Three sentences: what broke, why, what we changed.

## Impact

Who was affected, since when, and how we know (logs, queries, reports).
Say plainly what we do *not* know.

## Root cause

The chain of events, from the code that was wrong to the symptom the user
saw. Include the line(s) and, where it helps, a minimal snippet.

## Why it was not caught

The missing test, the misleading name, the assumption that did not hold.
Blameless: describe the system, not the person.

## The fix

What changed and why this change rather than the alternatives you
considered (list them in one line each).

## Verification

Tests added, manual checks performed, data checked after deploy.

## Follow-ups

| Action | Owner | Ticket |
|---|---|---|
| | | |

## References

Links to documentation, issues and articles used, one line each on why.
docs/templates/customer-update.md 
# Update for <customer / support agent> — <ticket id>

> **Audience:** non-engineers. No class names, no stack traces, no jargon.
> Read it aloud: if a sentence needs an engineer to explain it, rewrite it.

Hi <name>,

**What happened.** <One or two sentences in the customer's terms.
"The times on your sign-in history were shown an hour early.">

**Were you affected, and is your account safe?** <Answer the question they
are actually worried about, first and directly.>

**What we've done.** <The fix, in outcome terms. "Times now show correctly
in your own time zone.">

**Anything you need to do.** <Usually "Nothing." If there is something,
make it a numbered list of steps.>

**If you see it again.** <What to send us: a screenshot, the time it
happened and your time zone.>

Thanks for reporting it. Your report included <the detail that helped>,
which is what let us find it quickly.

<signature>

Part V · Rehearsal

Chapter 25 · Katas and Timed Drills

Reading about a timed test does not prepare you for one. This chapter is a practice schedule: four exercises, each against the clock, each scored with a rubric built from the test’s own criteria.

25.1 The exercises

# Exercise Time Where Skill
1 Page access kata 40 min katas/PageAccessKata Scenario 2
2 Access log kata 25 min katas/AccessLogKata Fundamentals: parsing, dictionaries, edge cases
3 Lab 1 and Lab 2 35 min each lab/* branches Scenario 1
4 Security page drill 25 min drill/angular-security-start Scenario 3

Do each at least twice, a few days apart. The second attempt is where the habits form.

25.2 Kata 1: which pages may each user open?

katas/PageAccessKata/README.md 
# Kata 1 — Which pages may each user open? (40 minutes)

A practice problem in the *shape* of the skill test's second scenario. It is
not the test's problem (that is confidential and unknown to this book); it
exercises the same muscles: modelling, iteration, dictionaries, edge cases,
naming, tests and comments for a reviewer.

## The brief

You are given users and pages.

- A **user** has a name and a list of role names.
- A **page** has a path (`/reports/finance`), an optional parent path, and a
  list of role names that may open it.

Return, for every user, the paths of the pages they may open, sorted
alphabetically.

Rules:

1. A page with **no required roles** may be opened by any user.
2. A page with required roles may be opened by a user holding **any one** of them.
3. A user may only open a page if they may also open its **parent** (and so on, up to the root).
4. The role `admin` may open every page that exists.
5. Role names are **case-insensitive**. Paths are compared case-insensitively and
   without a trailing slash; return them as given in the page list.

Edge cases the reviewer will look for (decide, implement, and comment):

- a page whose parent does not exist;
- two pages with the same path;
- a user with no roles, or a `null` role list;
- a parent cycle (`/a` → `/b` → `/a`);
- an empty list of users or pages.

## Working it

```powershell
# Your attempt: implement Starter/StarterPageAccessChecker.cs, then
dotnet test katas/Katas.slnx --filter "Category=Starter"

# The model answer's tests (always green):
dotnet test katas/Katas.slnx --filter "Category!=Starter"
```

Set a 40-minute timer. Write a comment at the top of your class listing the
decisions you made about each edge case — that comment is worth as much as
the code. Then compare with `Solution/SolutionPageAccessChecker.cs` and
Chapter 25.
katas/PageAccessKata/Model.cs 
namespace PageAccessKata;

public sealed record KataUser(string Name, IReadOnlyList<string>? Roles);

public sealed record KataPage(string Path, string? ParentPath, IReadOnlyList<string>? RequiredRoles);

public interface IPageAccessChecker
{
    /// <summary>User name -> accessible page paths, sorted alphabetically.</summary>
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IReadOnlyList<string>> AccessiblePagesByUser(
        IEnumerable<KataUser> users,
        IEnumerable<KataPage> pages);
}

The tests, shared by your starter and the model answer:

katas/PageAccessKata.Tests/PageAccessCheckerTests.cs 
using PageAccessKata.Solution;
using PageAccessKata.Starter;

namespace PageAccessKata.Tests;

/// <summary>
/// One set of tests, run against two implementations. Your starter must
/// pass exactly what the model answer passes.
/// </summary>
public abstract class PageAccessCheckerTests
{
    protected abstract IPageAccessChecker CreateChecker();

    private static readonly KataPage[] Site =
    [
        new("/", null, []),
        new("/reports", "/", ["analyst", "manager"]),
        new("/reports/finance", "/reports", ["manager"]),
        new("/admin", "/", ["it"]),
        new("/help", null, null),
    ];

    private IReadOnlyList<string> PagesFor(KataUser user, IEnumerable<KataPage>? pages = null) =>
        CreateChecker().AccessiblePagesByUser([user], pages ?? Site)[user.Name];

    [Fact]
    public void Pages_without_required_roles_are_open_to_everyone()
    {
        Assert.Equal(["/", "/help"], PagesFor(new KataUser("guest", [])));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Any_one_required_role_is_enough()
    {
        Assert.Equal(["/", "/help", "/reports"], PagesFor(new KataUser("ana", ["analyst"])));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void A_child_needs_its_parent()
    {
        var pages = new KataPage[] { new("/", null, []), new("/reports", "/", ["analyst"]), new("/reports/finance", "/reports", ["manager"]) };

        // manager without analyst: finance is allowed by role but sits behind /reports.
        Assert.Equal(["/"], PagesFor(new KataUser("mo", ["manager"]), pages));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Admin_sees_every_page()
    {
        Assert.Equal(["/", "/admin", "/help", "/reports", "/reports/finance"], PagesFor(new KataUser("root", ["admin"])));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Role_names_and_paths_ignore_case_and_trailing_slashes()
    {
        var pages = new KataPage[] { new("/", null, []), new("/Reports/", "/", ["Analyst"]), new("/reports/finance", "/REPORTS", [" analyst "]) };

        Assert.Equal(["/", "/Reports/", "/reports/finance"], PagesFor(new KataUser("ana", ["ANALYST"]), pages));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Null_role_list_is_treated_as_no_roles()
    {
        Assert.Equal(["/", "/help"], PagesFor(new KataUser("nobody", null)));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Missing_parent_denies_the_page_even_to_admin()
    {
        var pages = new KataPage[] { new("/orphan", "/gone", []) };

        Assert.Empty(PagesFor(new KataUser("root", ["admin"]), pages));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void A_parent_cycle_denies_every_page_on_it()
    {
        var pages = new KataPage[] { new("/a", "/b", []), new("/b", "/a", []), new("/c", "/a", []) };

        Assert.Empty(PagesFor(new KataUser("root", ["admin"]), pages));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void The_first_definition_of_a_duplicated_path_wins()
    {
        var pages = new KataPage[] { new("/x", null, []), new("/X", null, ["it"]) };

        Assert.Equal(["/x"], PagesFor(new KataUser("guest", []), pages));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Every_user_gets_an_entry_even_if_it_is_empty()
    {
        var result = CreateChecker().AccessiblePagesByUser([new KataUser("a", []), new KataUser("b", ["it"])], []);

        Assert.Equal(2, result.Count);
        Assert.All(result.Values, Assert.Empty);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void No_users_means_an_empty_result()
    {
        Assert.Empty(CreateChecker().AccessiblePagesByUser([], Site));
    }
}

{

Running one test class against two implementations is the Liskov substitution principle used as a teaching device: anything that satisfies IPageAccessChecker must pass the same tests.

Do the kata now, before reading the model answer.

katas/PageAccessKata/Solution/SolutionPageAccessChecker.cs 
namespace PageAccessKata.Solution;

/// <summary>
/// A model answer, written the way you would write it in the test: one
/// public method, small private helpers, and the decisions stated up front.
/// </summary>
/// <remarks>
/// Decisions (each is a choice the brief left open; a reviewer wants to see
/// that you noticed it and chose on purpose):
/// <list type="bullet">
///   <item>Missing parent: the page is inaccessible. Failing closed is the safe default for access control.</item>
///   <item>Duplicate paths: the first definition wins and later ones are ignored. Throwing would also be defensible; ignoring keeps one bad row from hiding every page.</item>
///   <item>Null role lists are treated as empty. Role names are trimmed and compared ignoring case.</item>
///   <item>Parent cycles: every page on or below the cycle is inaccessible, even to admin (it can never be reached by navigation).</item>
///   <item>Admin bypasses role checks but not structure: an orphan is still inaccessible to admin.</item>
///   <item>Duplicate user names: the last one wins in the result dictionary. Names are assumed unique.</item>
/// </list>
/// Complexity: O(users × pages × depth) in the worst case; each page's
/// ancestry is resolved once per user thanks to memoisation.
/// </remarks>
public sealed class SolutionPageAccessChecker : IPageAccessChecker
{
    private const string AdminRole = "admin";

    public IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IReadOnlyList<string>> AccessiblePagesByUser(
        IEnumerable<KataUser> users,
        IEnumerable<KataPage> pages)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(users);
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(pages);

        var pagesByPath = IndexPages(pages);
        var result = new Dictionary<string, IReadOnlyList<string>>();

        foreach (var user in users)
        {
            var roles = new HashSet<string>(
                (user.Roles ?? []).Where(r => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(r)).Select(r => r.Trim()),
                StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

            var memo = new Dictionary<string, bool>();
            result[user.Name] = pagesByPath.Values
                .Where(page => CanOpen(page, roles, pagesByPath, memo, visiting: []))
                .Select(page => page.Path)
                .Order(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
                .ToList();
        }

        return result;
    }

    private static Dictionary<string, KataPage> IndexPages(IEnumerable<KataPage> pages)
    {
        var index = new Dictionary<string, KataPage>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        foreach (var page in pages)
        {
            index.TryAdd(Normalise(page.Path), page); // first definition wins
        }
        return index;
    }

    private static bool CanOpen(
        KataPage page,
        HashSet<string> roles,
        Dictionary<string, KataPage> pagesByPath,
        Dictionary<string, bool> memo,
        HashSet<string> visiting)
    {
        var key = Normalise(page.Path);
        if (memo.TryGetValue(key, out var known))
            return known;

        // Seen on the way up: we are walking in a circle.
        if (!visiting.Add(key))
            return false;

        var allowed = ParentAllows(page, roles, pagesByPath, memo, visiting) && RolesAllow(page, roles);

        visiting.Remove(key);
        memo[key] = allowed;
        return allowed;
    }

    private static bool ParentAllows(
        KataPage page,
        HashSet<string> roles,
        Dictionary<string, KataPage> pagesByPath,
        Dictionary<string, bool> memo,
        HashSet<string> visiting)
    {
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(page.ParentPath))
            return true;

        return pagesByPath.TryGetValue(Normalise(page.ParentPath), out var parent)
            && CanOpen(parent, roles, pagesByPath, memo, visiting);
    }

    private static bool RolesAllow(KataPage page, HashSet<string> roles)
    {
        var required = (page.RequiredRoles ?? []).Where(r => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(r)).ToList();
        return required.Count == 0
            || roles.Contains(AdminRole)
            || required.Any(r => roles.Contains(r.Trim()));
    }

    /// <summary>"/Reports/" -> "/reports". The root "/" stays "/".</summary>
    private static string Normalise(string path)
    {
        var trimmed = path.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();
        return trimmed.Length > 1 ? trimmed.TrimEnd('/') : trimmed;
    }
}

What to compare with your attempt:

  • Is there a “Decisions” comment, and does it cover every edge case in the brief?
  • Is the input indexed once (Dictionary) rather than searched in a loop?
  • Are the rules in small named functions (ParentAllows, RolesAllow)?
  • Is the cycle handled, and how? (visiting set.)
  • Is anything hard-coded that should be a named constant? (AdminRole.)
  • Did you add tests for decisions the provided tests did not cover?

25.3 Kata 2: summarise an access log

katas/AccessLogKata/README.md 
# Kata 2 — Summarise an access log (25 minutes)

Warm-up practice for the fundamentals the prep guide lists: iterating,
dictionaries, converting strings to numbers and dates, and handling input
that is not what you expected.

## The brief

Each line of the log looks like this:

```
2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,ada,/reports/finance,ALLOW,142
```

timestamp (ISO 8601, must include a zone), user, path, decision (`ALLOW` or
`DENY`, any case), and the response time in milliseconds (a non-negative
integer).

Write `Summarise(IEnumerable<string> lines)` returning:

- per user: allowed count, denied count, and **average** response time (ms, as a `double`);
- the path with the most denials (ties: alphabetical first; none: `null`);
- the 1-based line numbers of every malformed line, which are otherwise ignored.

Blank lines and lines starting with `#` are comments, not errors.
User names are case-insensitive (`Ada` and `ada` are one user, reported in
lower case).

```powershell
dotnet test katas/Katas.slnx --filter "Category=Starter&FullyQualifiedName~AccessLog"
```
katas/AccessLogKata/Model.cs 
namespace AccessLogKata;

public sealed record UserActivity(int Allowed, int Denied, double AverageResponseMs);

public sealed record LogSummary(
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, UserActivity> ByUser,
    string? MostDeniedPath,
    IReadOnlyList<int> MalformedLines);

public interface IAccessLogSummariser
{
    LogSummary Summarise(IEnumerable<string> lines);
}
katas/AccessLogKata.Tests/AccessLogSummariserTests.cs 
using AccessLogKata.Solution;
using AccessLogKata.Starter;

namespace AccessLogKata.Tests;

public abstract class AccessLogSummariserTests
{
    protected abstract IAccessLogSummariser Create();

    [Fact]
    public void Counts_and_averages_per_user()
    {
        var summary = Create().Summarise(
        [
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,ada,/reports,ALLOW,100",
            "2026-10-24T08:01:00Z,Ada,/admin,DENY,50",
            "2026-10-24T08:02:00+01:00,bola,/reports,allow,30",
        ]);

        Assert.Equal(new UserActivity(1, 1, 75), summary.ByUser["ada"]);
        Assert.Equal(new UserActivity(1, 0, 30), summary.ByUser["bola"]);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Most_denied_path_breaks_ties_alphabetically()
    {
        var summary = Create().Summarise(
        [
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,a,/z,DENY,1",
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,a,/b,DENY,1",
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,a,/z,ALLOW,1",
        ]);

        Assert.Equal("/b", summary.MostDeniedPath);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void No_denials_means_no_most_denied_path()
    {
        Assert.Null(Create().Summarise(["2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,a,/z,ALLOW,1"]).MostDeniedPath);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Malformed_lines_are_reported_by_number_and_otherwise_ignored()
    {
        var summary = Create().Summarise(
        [
            "# header comment",
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,ada,/reports,ALLOW,100",
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00,ada,/reports,ALLOW,100",   // 3: no zone
            "not,a,log,line",                                // 4: four fields
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,ada,/reports,MAYBE,100",  // 5: bad decision
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,ada,/reports,ALLOW,-5",   // 6: negative
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,ada,/reports,ALLOW,1,000",// 7: six fields
            "",
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,,/reports,ALLOW,1",       // 9: no user
            "2026-10-24T08:00:00Z,ada,reports,ALLOW,1",     // 10: not a path
        ]);

        Assert.Equal([3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10], summary.MalformedLines);
        Assert.Equal(new UserActivity(1, 0, 100), Assert.Single(summary.ByUser).Value);
    }

    [Fact]
    public void An_empty_log_is_an_empty_summary()
    {
        var summary = Create().Summarise([]);

        Assert.Empty(summary.ByUser);
        Assert.Empty(summary.MalformedLines);
        Assert.Null(summary.MostDeniedPath);
    }
}

katas/AccessLogKata/Solution/SolutionAccessLogSummariser.cs 
using System.Globalization;

namespace AccessLogKata.Solution;

/// <summary>
/// Model answer. Parsing and aggregating are separate steps: a line either
/// becomes a well-typed <see cref="Entry"/> or a line number in the error
/// list, and the aggregation never sees a string.
/// </summary>
public sealed class SolutionAccessLogSummariser : IAccessLogSummariser
{
    private sealed record Entry(DateTimeOffset At, string User, string Path, bool Allowed, int ResponseMs);

    private sealed class Totals
    {
        public int Allowed;
        public int Denied;
        public long ResponseMsSum;
    }

    public LogSummary Summarise(IEnumerable<string> lines)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(lines);

        var byUser = new Dictionary<string, Totals>();
        var deniesByPath = new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.Ordinal);
        var malformed = new List<int>();

        var lineNumber = 0;
        foreach (var line in lines)
        {
            lineNumber++;
            if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(line) || line.TrimStart().StartsWith('#'))
                continue;

            if (TryParse(line) is not { } entry)
            {
                malformed.Add(lineNumber);
                continue;
            }

            if (!byUser.TryGetValue(entry.User, out var totals))
                byUser[entry.User] = totals = new Totals();

            totals.ResponseMsSum += entry.ResponseMs; // long: a busy day of ints can overflow int
            if (entry.Allowed)
            {
                totals.Allowed++;
            }
            else
            {
                totals.Denied++;
                deniesByPath[entry.Path] = deniesByPath.GetValueOrDefault(entry.Path) + 1;
            }
        }

        var mostDenied = deniesByPath
            .OrderByDescending(kv => kv.Value)
            .ThenBy(kv => kv.Key, StringComparer.Ordinal)
            .Select(kv => kv.Key)
            .FirstOrDefault();

        var activity = byUser.ToDictionary(
            kv => kv.Key,
            kv => new UserActivity(kv.Value.Allowed, kv.Value.Denied,
                (double)kv.Value.ResponseMsSum / (kv.Value.Allowed + kv.Value.Denied)));

        return new LogSummary(activity, mostDenied, malformed);
    }

    private static Entry? TryParse(string line)
    {
        var parts = line.Split(',');
        if (parts.Length != 5)
            return null;

        var (timestamp, user, path, decision, response) = (parts[0].Trim(), parts[1].Trim(), parts[2].Trim(), parts[3].Trim(), parts[4].Trim());

        // A timestamp without a zone is ambiguous; refuse it rather than guess.
        if (!timestamp.EndsWith('Z') && !HasOffset(timestamp))
            return null;

        if (!DateTimeOffset.TryParse(timestamp, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.None, out var at))
            return null;

        if (user.Length == 0 || !path.StartsWith('/'))
            return null;

        bool allowed;
        if (decision.Equals("ALLOW", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) allowed = true;
        else if (decision.Equals("DENY", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) allowed = false;
        else return null;

        // NumberStyles.None: no sign, no spaces, no thousands separators: "-5" and "1,000" are malformed.
        if (!int.TryParse(response, NumberStyles.None, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out var ms))
            return null;

        return new Entry(at, user.ToLowerInvariant(), path, allowed, ms);
    }

    private static bool HasOffset(string timestamp) =>
        timestamp.Length > 6 && (timestamp[^6] == '+' || timestamp[^6] == '-') && timestamp[^3] == ':';
}

The patterns to take away: parse into a typed record or reject, so the aggregation never sees a string; NumberStyles.None and CultureInfo.InvariantCulture so that -5, 1,000 and a French machine’s decimal comma do not surprise you; long for sums that can outgrow int; and GetValueOrDefault(key) + 1 as the idiomatic dictionary counter.

Chapter 25 lists what a reviewer looks for. Score yourself honestly.

25.5 The rubric

Score each attempt honestly, 0 to 2 per line (0 absent, 1 partly, 2 clearly). The lines are the prep guide’s criteria, made concrete.

Coding (katas, drill)

Criterion 2 points looks like
Core requirements Every rule in the brief is implemented and visibly traceable to the code
Edge cases Each listed edge case has a decision, a comment and a test
Names A reader could guess each function’s body from its name
Structure One entry point; helpers of 5–20 lines; no magic strings or numbers
Tests At least three tests beyond those provided, each for a decision
Comments A “Decisions”/trade-offs comment; no comments that restate the code
(Angular) Passing data Inputs down, outputs up, one container with the side effects
(Angular) Dates Parsed strictly, formatted in the user’s zone, relative time testable

Debugging (labs)

Criterion 2 points looks like
Gathering Reproduced at the lowest level; evidence before conclusions
Research Precise searches, primary sources, every source cited
Documenting A log a colleague could continue from
To engineers Cause, fix, why missed, follow-ups, in under a page
To non-engineers Answers the reader’s worry first; one clear action; no jargon

Fourteen or more out of sixteen on the coding rubric, and nine or more out of ten on the debugging one, and you are ready.

Chapter 26 · Test Day

26.1 The day before

26.2 Before each scenario

26.3 Inside the authorisation scenario (40 min)

  1. Requirements as a numbered comment.
  2. Edge cases as a table in the comment, each with a decision.
  3. Index the input; one function per rule; a cycle guard if there is a hierarchy.
  4. Run the provided tests early and often.
  5. A test per edge-case decision.
  6. Names, constants, the “Decisions” comment. If something advanced is beyond the time, use what you know and say so in a comment.

26.4 Inside the debugging scenario (35 min)

  1. Copy the report; facts, assumptions, unknowns; questions for the reporter.
  2. Reproduce at the lowest level.
  3. Hypotheses, cheapest test first. Cite every source.
  4. At minute 22: found it → test, fix; not found → write up what you ruled out.
  5. Ten minutes for two write-ups. Protect this time.

26.5 Inside the Angular scenario (25 min)

  1. Sketch the component tree in a comment: container, children, inputs, outputs.
  2. Get correct data on screen first.
  3. Dates: strict parsing, the user’s zone, Intl, relative time with a passed-in “now”.
  4. Edge cases: empty, loading, error, unknown values, singular/plural.
  5. If you use AI, cite it in a comment and say what you changed.

26.6 Citing, in practice

// Two-pointer sliding window adapted from:
// https://learn.microsoft.com/... (or the Stack Overflow answer's permalink)
// Suggested by an AI assistant (2026-10-26) for Intl.RelativeTimeFormat units;
// changed to take `now` as a parameter for testability.

26.7 After

Woven promises detailed feedback whatever the outcome. Read it against the rubric in §25.5, find the two lowest lines, and practise those. Whatever the result, you will have built, tested and debugged a real application, and that stays with you.

Appendix A · C# Fundamentals for the Test

The prep guide lists fundamentals to review. Here each one is, in C#, with an example from Sentinel’s domain.

A.1 Iteration

// for: when you need the index
for (var i = 0; i < attempts.Count; i++) { var attempt = attempts[i]; }

// foreach: the default
foreach (var attempt in attempts) { if (!attempt.Succeeded) failures++; }

// LINQ: when the loop computes a value
var failures = attempts.Count(a => !a.Succeeded);
var countries = attempts.Where(a => a.Succeeded).Select(a => a.Location.CountryCode).Distinct().ToList();
var newestFirst = attempts.OrderByDescending(a => a.OccurredAtUtc).ToList();
var byUser = attempts.GroupBy(a => a.UserId).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count());

// while: when the end condition is not a count (see MaxInAnyWindow)
while (burst[end].OccurredAtUtc - burst[start].OccurredAtUtc > window) start++;

LINQ is lazy: a query runs when it is enumerated (ToList, foreach, Count). Enumerating it twice runs it twice. Call ToList() once when you will use the result more than once.

A.2 Inspecting values

Console.WriteLine($"[debug] user={user.Name} roles={string.Join(",", user.Roles ?? [])}");

In xUnit, output from tests goes through ITestOutputHelper (constructor-injected) rather than Console. Remove debug output before submitting.

A.3 Classes and objects

public sealed class Role                     // a class with behaviour and identity
{
    private readonly List<string> _permissions = [];
    public Role(string name) => Name = name;  // constructor
    public string Name { get; }               // get-only property
    public IReadOnlyList<string> Permissions => _permissions;
    public void Grant(string p) => _permissions.Add(p);   // a method
}

var role = new Role("Auditor");               // initialise
role.Grant("reports.view");                   // call a method
Console.WriteLine(role.Name);                 // get a property

public sealed record KataPage(string Path, string? ParentPath, IReadOnlyList<string>? RequiredRoles);
var page = new KataPage("/reports", "/", ["analyst"]);   // records: value equality, concise
var moved = page with { ParentPath = "/home" };           // non-destructive copy

A.4 Collections

Need Type Key operations
Fixed sequence T[] index, Length
Growable list List<T> Add, Remove, Count, index
Lookup by key Dictionary<TKey, TValue> TryGetValue, TryAdd, GetValueOrDefault, ContainsKey
Membership HashSet<T> Add (returns false if present), Contains
Read-only view IReadOnlyList<T>, IReadOnlyDictionary<,> expose, don’t mutate

Case-insensitive keys: new Dictionary<string, Page>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase). Counting idiom: counts[key] = counts.GetValueOrDefault(key) + 1;

A.5 Converting between types

int.TryParse("142", NumberStyles.None, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out var ms);   // never int.Parse on input
DateTimeOffset.TryParse("2026-10-24T08:00:00Z", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, DateTimeStyles.None, out var at);
Enum.TryParse<PermissionEffect>("deny", ignoreCase: true, out var effect);           // also accepts "1"! check Enum.IsDefined
var asText = ms.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
var utc = at.UtcDateTime;                                                             // DateTimeOffset -> DateTime (Kind=Utc)

Always pass CultureInfo.InvariantCulture when parsing machine data. A machine set to French parses 1,5 as one and a half.

A.6 Null handling

var roles = user.Roles ?? [];                        // default for null
var city = attempt?.Location?.City ?? "Unknown";     // null-conditional chain
ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(pages);            // programming errors fail fast
if (page.ParentId is { } parentId) { ... }           // pattern: non-null and bind

Appendix B · TypeScript and JavaScript Fundamentals for the Test

B.1 Iteration

for (let i = 0; i < signIns.length; i++) { const s = signIns[i]; }
for (const s of signIns) { if (!s.succeeded) failures++; }     // for...of: values
for (const key in record) { }                                   // for...in: keys of an object (rarely what you want)

const failed = signIns.filter((s) => !s.succeeded);
const ids = signIns.map((s) => s.id);
const firstFlagged = signIns.find((s) => s.isFlagged);          // undefined if none
const count = signIns.reduce((n, s) => n + (s.isFlagged ? 1 : 0), 0);

B.2 Inspecting values

console.log('[security] status', status);          // objects are expandable in dev tools
console.table(status.recentSignIns);               // arrays of objects as a table

B.3 Classes and objects

class FindingCounter {
  private readonly counts = new Map<string, number>();
  constructor(private readonly label: string) {}      // parameter property
  add(kind: string): void { this.counts.set(kind, (this.counts.get(kind) ?? 0) + 1); }
  get total(): number { return [...this.counts.values()].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }
}

const counter = new FindingCounter('today');
counter.add('NewDevice');
console.log(counter.total);

const finding = { key: 'x', severity: 'High' };       // object literal
finding.severity = 'Low';                              // set a property
const copy = { ...finding, key: 'y' };                 // copy with a change

B.4 Arrays, maps, objects as dictionaries

Need Use
Ordered list T[] (push, length, includes, indexOf)
Lookup by key Map<K, V> (get, set, has), or Record<string, V> for fixed keys
Membership Set<T> (add, has)

B.5 Converting between types

Number('142');                 // 142; Number('') is 0, Number('abc') is NaN
parseInt('142px', 10);         // 142 (stops at the first non-digit)
Number.isNaN(value);           // the only reliable NaN check
String(42); `${42}`;           // to string
JSON.parse(text);              // string -> object (throws on bad JSON)
new Date('2026-10-24T08:00:00Z');   // ALWAYS with a Z or an offset
date.toISOString();            // Date -> UTC string with Z

B.6 Equality and truthiness

Use === and !==. 0, '', null, undefined, NaN and false are falsy: count || 10 replaces a real 0; count ?? 10 does not.

Appendix D · Troubleshooting

Every entry below happened while this book was written.

Symptom Cause Fix
NU1903: Package 'System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs' 9.0.11 has a known high severity vulnerability A transitive dependency of the SQL Server provider, with warnings as errors Pin it centrally with CentralPackageTransitivePinningEnabled (§4.4)
NU1301: ... No such host is known (api.nuget.org) A transient network failure Retry; check proxy settings
Invalid object name 'Users' on start-up The API was run with --no-build before the migration was added, so the old assembly had no migrations Build, then run
CS8188: An expression tree may not contain a throw-expression throw inside a value converter lambda Move the check into a static method (§11.1)
CS8620 nullability mismatch on HasConversion for a nullable value object The generic overload’s nullability Cast to the non-generic ValueConverter (PageConfiguration)
npm error notarget No matching version found during ng new A package published moments earlier, not yet on the mirror Run npm install again in the workspace
proxy.conf.json contains parse errors: [1, 1] InvalidSymbol A UTF-8 byte-order mark from PowerShell 5’s Set-Content -Encoding utf8 Save without BOM
